fields.title: 2 Kings
fields.subtitle: Melakhim Bet, “Kings”
fields.description: The second half of the book of Kings, which carries the story of God’s people from the chariot of fire that took Elijah up to heaven to the burning of Jerusalem. Elisha takes up his master’s cloak: a widow’s oil flows until there are no more jars, a Shunammite’s son opens his eyes, Naaman washes seven times in the Jordan, and a frightened servant sees the hills full of horses and chariots of fire. Then the kingdoms fall, Samaria to Assyria and Jerusalem to Babylon, though not before Hezekiah spreads a threatening letter before the LORD and Josiah hears the book of the law and tears his clothes. It ends with a captive son of David released from prison to eat at the king’s table. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of 2 Kings?
qa.answer: The second half of the book of Kings in the Old Testament, which in Hebrew is a single book called Melakhim, “Kings”. Its twenty-five chapters run from the middle of the ninth century BC to about 561 BC. Chapters 1–8 tell of the prophet Elisha; chapters 9–17 follow the kingdoms of Israel and Judah to the fall of Samaria to Assyria in 722 BC; and chapters 18–25 follow Judah alone, through the reigns of Hezekiah, Manasseh and Josiah, to the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon in 586 BC and the release of King Jehoiachin in exile.

qa.question: Who wrote 2 Kings, and when?
qa.answer: The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition, recorded in the Talmud, credited Kings to the prophet Jeremiah, and the last chapter of Jeremiah repeats the end of 2 Kings almost word for word. Many scholars think the book was completed during the exile in Babylon, since its last event, Jehoiachin’s release, can be dated to about 561 BC, and some think an earlier edition was made in the days of King Josiah. It draws on older royal records it names, the histories of the kings of Israel and of Judah.

qa.question: Why were Israel and Judah sent into exile?
qa.answer: 2 Kings answers the question directly in chapter 17, after the fall of Samaria: the people had worshipped other gods and refused to listen to the prophets the LORD sent them again and again, warning them to turn back. It says the same of Judah, especially after the long reign of Manasseh (21:10–15; 24:3–4). The book stresses that judgement came only after centuries of patience, and that even then God kept his promise to David alive in the person of the exiled king Jehoiachin.

qa.question: What is the story of Naaman in 2 Kings 5?
qa.answer: Naaman was commander of the army of Aram, an enemy of Israel, and he had a serious skin disease, traditionally called leprosy. On the advice of a captive Israelite girl he came to the prophet Elisha, who sent word that he should wash seven times in the Jordan. Naaman was offended by so plain a command, but his servants persuaded him, and he was made clean and confessed that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel. Jesus cited him in Luke 4:27 as one of the foreigners to whom God showed mercy.

qa.question: What happened to Elijah in 2 Kings 2?
qa.answer: As Elijah and his successor Elisha walked on together beyond the Jordan, a chariot of fire with horses of fire came between them, and Elijah went up to heaven in a whirlwind (2:11). Elijah did not die, which is one reason later Jewish hope expected his return before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5). Elisha, who had asked for a double portion of his spirit, took up the cloak Elijah left behind and struck the Jordan, and the water parted for him as it had for his master.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. “LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Yet the LORD warned Israel and Judah through every prophet and every seer: “Turn back from your evil ways. Keep my commandments and my statutes, in keeping with the whole law that I commanded your ancestors and sent to you through my servants the prophets.”

— 2 Kings 17:13

2 Kings begins with a king who has fallen through the lattice of his upper room and sends to ask a foreign god whether he will recover. Elijah meets his messengers on the road with a question: “Are you going to consult Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, because there is no God in Israel?” It ends, twenty-five chapters later, with the last king of David’s line in Babylon, released from prison and given a seat at the conqueror’s table. Between those two scenes, both kingdoms of God’s people are lost.

It is the second half of the book the Hebrew Bible calls Melakhim, “Kings”, divided in two by the ancient Greek translation; it picks up the story in the middle of a reign. It runs from the middle of the ninth century BC to about 561 BC: through the fall of Samaria to Assyria in 722 BC and the burning of Jerusalem by Babylon in 586 BC. It is the story of how the people who were promised a land came to be carried out of it.

But it is not only a story of loss. It holds some of the most beloved scenes in the Old Testament: a chariot of fire, a widow’s jar of oil that will not run dry, a foreign general washing seven times in the Jordan, a servant who sees the hills full of fire. And it never stops saying why the end came, and that it came only after long patience.

Three movements

Chapters 1–8 belong mostly to the prophet Elisha, Elijah’s successor, and are full of wonders done among ordinary people. Chapters 9–17 follow both kingdoms from Jehu’s bloody revolution to the fall of the northern kingdom, and pause to explain it. Chapters 18–25 follow Judah alone, through two great reforming kings, Hezekiah and Josiah, and one terrible one, Manasseh, to the fall of Jerusalem and a brief, quiet coda in Babylon.

“Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?”

Elijah’s last day is a farewell walk. From Gilgal to Bethel to Jericho to the Jordan, he tells Elisha to stay behind, and three times Elisha refuses: “As surely as the LORD lives and as surely as you live, I will not leave you.” Across the river, Elijah asks what he can do for him, and Elisha asks for “a double portion of your spirit”, the share an eldest son inherited from his father. Then:

As they were walking along and talking, suddenly a chariot of fire with horses of fire came between the two of them, and Elijah went up to heaven in the whirlwind.

— 2 Kings 2:11

Elisha cries out, “My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!” He picks up the cloak that fell from Elijah, goes back to the Jordan, strikes the water and asks, “Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?” The water divides. The prophet has gone, but the prophet’s God has not.

Not every Elisha story is comfortable. On the road up to Bethel, the centre of Jeroboam’s calf worship, a crowd of “young lads” mock him, and when he curses them in the LORD’s name two bears come out of the forest and maul forty-two of them. Readers have long struggled with the scene. Some note that the Hebrew words can describe young men rather than small children, and that the mockery was aimed at the LORD’s prophet at the heart of rebellion against him; even so, it remains a hard story, told without comment.

The man of God among ordinary people

Most of Elisha’s wonders are done for people who would never appear in a royal chronicle. A prophet’s widow is about to lose her two sons to a creditor, and has nothing in the house but “a small jar of oil”. Elisha tells her to borrow empty containers from all her neighbours, “and not just a few”, and to start pouring. The oil flows until she asks for another, and her son tells her, “There are no more.” “Then the oil stopped flowing.” God’s supply was limited only by the room she made for it.

A wealthy woman in Shunem builds a little room on her roof for the prophet, with “a bed, a table, a chair and a lamp”. She is given a son, and when the boy dies in her lap she rides straight to Elisha and will not leave him. He lies on the child, mouth to mouth and hands to hands, and “The boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes.” Twenty loaves feed a hundred men, “and there was some left over, as the LORD had said.” An axe head, borrowed and lost in the Jordan, floats. These are small mercies, and they foreshadow greater ones: the New Testament’s readers would recognise a man of God who feeds a crowd with a few loaves, raises a mother’s only son and cleanses a leper.

Naaman

The most famous of these stories is about an enemy. Naaman, commander of the army of Aram, is a great man and a mighty warrior, but he has a serious skin disease. A captive Israelite girl who serves his wife tells her mistress about the prophet in Samaria. Naaman arrives at Elisha’s door with horses, chariots and a fortune in gifts, and Elisha does not even come out. He sends a messenger: “Go and wash seven times in the Jordan.” Naaman storms off in a rage. Are not the rivers of Damascus better? Then his servants reason with him:

His servants came up to him and said, “My father, had the prophet asked you to do something great, would you not have done it? How much more, then, should you obey when he tells you only, ‘Wash and be clean’!”

— 2 Kings 5:13

He goes down to the Jordan, and his flesh becomes “like the flesh of a young boy”. He returns, a different man, to confess, “Now I know that in all the earth there is no God except in Israel.” Jesus told the synagogue at Nazareth that of all the people with leprosy in Israel in Elisha’s time, only this Syrian was made clean (Luke 4:27), and they tried to throw him off a cliff for it. Grace, then as now, is not earned and not limited to insiders. Elisha’s servant Gehazi, who runs after Naaman to collect the gifts his master refused, goes away with the disease himself.

The same generosity shows in war. When an Aramean army surrounds Elisha’s town, his servant panics: “Oh no, my master! What shall we do?” Elisha prays:

Then Elisha prayed, “LORD, please open his eyes so that he can see.” The LORD opened the young man’s eyes, and he saw that the hill was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha.

— 2 Kings 6:17

The raiders are led, blinded, into Samaria, and the king of Israel asks whether he should kill them. “Do not kill them,” Elisha answers. “Set food and water before them, so that they can eat and drink and then go back to their master.” The king gives them a feast and sends them home, “And the Aramean raiding bands did not come into the land of Israel again.” It is the Old Testament’s own picture of loving one’s enemies.

Jehu and the lamp in Jerusalem

Elisha sends a young prophet to anoint Jehu, an army commander, as king of Israel, with orders to destroy the house of Ahab. Jehu, who “drives like a madman”, does it with a thoroughness that leaves Jezebel dead beneath her window, Ahab’s seventy sons beheaded and the worshippers of Baal slaughtered in their own temple. On the way he meets Jehonadab and asks, “Is your heart right with mine, as my heart is with yours?”, the question John Wesley would take for one of his best-loved sermons.

The verdict on Jehu is mixed. “So Jehu wiped out Baal worship from Israel,” and the LORD commends him; but “Jehu took no care to walk in the law of the LORD, the God of Israel, with his whole heart”, and he kept Jeroboam’s golden calves. Nearly a century later the prophet Hosea would announce judgement on Jehu’s house “for the blood shed at Jezreel” (Hosea 1:4). Zeal for God is not the same as a whole heart.

In Judah, meanwhile, David’s lamp nearly goes out. When her son the king is killed, Athaliah, a daughter of Ahab’s house, sets out to destroy the whole royal family. One baby, Joash, is rescued by his aunt and hidden in the temple for six years. Then the priest Jehoiada brings him out, crowns him, and makes a covenant “that they would be the people of the LORD.” The whole promise to David had hung on one hidden child.

The fall of Samaria

The northern kingdom’s last decades are a blur of assassinations. Even then God was patient: when Israel was suffering bitterly, he “was gracious to them and had compassion on them”, and through the prophet Jonah son of Amittai he promised to restore its borders. But in 722 BC the king of Assyria captured Samaria and carried its people into exile.

Here the narrator stops and preaches. Chapter 17 is the theological heart of Kings. “This happened because the Israelites had sinned against the LORD their God.” They had worshipped other gods; they had ignored the prophets the LORD sent “through every prophet and every seer”; “They went after worthless idols and became worthless themselves.” Then the king of Assyria resettled the land with peoples from far away, who learned to fear the LORD while keeping their own gods, often seen as the beginning of the long division between Jews and Samaritans that still stands in the background of John 4. The sermon is addressed to Judah too: “Even Judah failed to keep the commandments of the LORD their God.”

Hezekiah

Then comes a king like David. Hezekiah tears down the high places and even breaks up the bronze snake Moses had made, because the people had made it an idol. “He trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel.” In 701 BC, Sennacherib of Assyria sweeps through Judah and sends his chief officer to stand outside Jerusalem’s walls and mock: “What sort of confidence is this that you are trusting in?” When a threatening letter arrives, Hezekiah does something unforgettable:

Hezekiah took the letter from the messengers’ hand and read it through. He went up to the house of the LORD and opened it out in the presence of the LORD.

— 2 Kings 19:14

He prays that “every kingdom on earth will know that you, LORD, alone are God.” Through Isaiah the answer comes that the king of Assyria will not enter the city, and that night the angel of the LORD strikes the Assyrian camp. Sennacherib’s own inscriptions, which survive, boast that he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem “like a bird in a cage”, and say nothing of taking the city.

When Hezekiah falls ill, he weeps and prays, and is told, “I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears,” and given fifteen more years. But he shows envoys from Babylon his whole treasury, and Isaiah warns that everything in it will one day be hauled off to Babylon. Hezekiah’s answer is chilling: “Is it not good, if there will be peace and stability as long as I live?” Even the best kings are not the King the promise needs. These chapters appear again, almost word for word, in Isaiah 36–39.

Manasseh and Josiah

Hezekiah’s son Manasseh reigns fifty-five years, longer than any other king of Judah, and undoes everything. He rebuilds the high places, worships the stars, sacrifices his own son and fills Jerusalem with innocent blood. The LORD says that he will bring such disaster on Jerusalem “that it will make both ears of all who hear of it tingle”, and wipe it clean “as someone wipes a dish”.

Then his grandson Josiah becomes king at eight years old, and during repairs to the temple the high priest makes a discovery: “In the house of the LORD I have found the book of the law.” When Josiah hears it read he tears his clothes. Many scholars think the book was Deuteronomy, or its core. Josiah sends to the prophet Huldah, then gathers the whole people, reads them the book of the covenant, and leads the greatest reform and the greatest Passover in Judah’s history. At Bethel he burns bones on Jeroboam’s altar, as the man of God had foretold three centuries before.

Before him there was no king like him, who turned to the LORD with his whole heart, with his whole being, and with all his strength, in keeping with all the law of Moses; and after him no one like him arose.

— 2 Kings 23:25

And yet the next verse begins, “Even so.” The reform came too late to turn away the judgement Manasseh’s reign had brought. Josiah was killed at Megiddo in 609 BC, and within a generation Babylon had come.

The fall of Jerusalem

The end is told with terrible economy. Nebuchadnezzar takes King Jehoiachin and ten thousand captives to Babylon in 597 BC. Eleven years later, after Zedekiah rebels, the city falls; Zedekiah is made to watch his sons killed before his eyes are put out; and the captain of the guard “burned the house of the LORD, the king’s palace and all the houses of Jerusalem”. “So Judah went into exile, away from its own land.”

And then, in the last four verses, a small door opens. In the thirty-seventh year of his exile, Jehoiachin is released from prison and given a seat of honour above the other captive kings, and “for the rest of his life he ate regularly at the king’s table.” Clay tablets from Babylon, found in the twentieth century, list the rations given to “Jehoiachin, king of Judah” and his sons. David’s line is in chains, but it is alive.

How to read 2 Kings

Read it as the second half of one book with 1 Kings. Take Elisha’s stories slowly, one at a time; then read chapters 17–25 straight through, because their cumulative weight is the point. Many of the prophets lived in these years, and their books open up the history from the inside: Jonah and Amos in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, Hosea in Israel’s last decades, Isaiah and Micah in Hezekiah’s, Jeremiah from Josiah to the fall. 2 Chronicles retells the Judean story from another angle and adds things Kings leaves out, including the repentance of Manasseh.

The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition credited Kings to Jeremiah, and the last chapter of Jeremiah repeats the end of 2 Kings almost exactly. Many scholars think the book reached its final form during the exile, since its last event can be dated to about 561 BC, and some think there was an earlier edition in Josiah’s day. Christians hold a range of views on its composition; all agree that it was written for people who had lost everything, to tell them why, and to show them that God had not finished with David’s house.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in 2 Kings are worth knowing.

“The LORD.” Where the Hebrew uses God’s personal name, this translation follows long custom and writes “the LORD”.

“Serious skin disease.” The Hebrew word traditionally translated “leprosy” covered a range of skin conditions, not only what is now called leprosy. This translation calls Naaman’s illness, and Gehazi’s, “a serious skin disease”.

“The company of prophets.” The groups older translations call “the sons of the prophets”, the bands of prophets gathered around Elijah and Elisha, appear as “the company of prophets”.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: 2 Kings 1
fields.body_html:
Elijah and King Ahaziah

After Ahab died, Moab rebelled against Israel. Ahaziah fell through the lattice of his upper room in Samaria and was injured. So he sent messengers, telling them, “Go and consult Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I will get over this injury.”

But the angel of the LORD said to Elijah the Tishbite, “Get up and go to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria. Say to them, ‘Are you going to consult Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, because there is no God in Israel? Now therefore the LORD says this: You will not come down from the bed you have gone up to; you will certainly die.’” So Elijah went. When the messengers came back to the king, he asked them, “Why have you come back?” They told him, “A man came up to meet us. He said, ‘Go back to the king who sent you and say to him, The LORD says this: Are you sending men to consult Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, because there is no God in Israel? For that reason you will not come down from the bed you have gone up to; you will certainly die.’” He asked them, “What kind of man was it who came up to meet you and told you these things?” They answered him, “He was a hairy man, with a leather belt tied around his waist.” And the king said, “It is Elijah the Tishbite.” Then the king sent a commander of fifty with his fifty men to Elijah. The commander went up to him, and there he was, sitting on top of the hill. He called to him, “Man of God, the king says, ‘Come down!’” Elijah answered the commander of the fifty, “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and devour you and your fifty men!” Then fire came down from heaven and consumed him and his fifty men. The king sent to him another commander of fifty with his fifty men. This one spoke up and said to him, “Man of God, the king says this: Come down at once!” Elijah answered them, “If I am the man of God, let fire come down from heaven and devour you and your fifty men!” Then the fire of God fell from heaven and consumed him and his fifty men. Then the king sent a third commander of fifty with his fifty men. This third commander went up, fell on his knees before Elijah and pleaded with him: “Man of God, please let my life, and the lives of these fifty servants of yours, be precious to you. Fire has come down from heaven and consumed the first two commanders of fifty and their fifty men. But now let my life be precious to you.”

Ahaziah dies

The angel of the LORD told Elijah, “Go down with him, and have no fear of him.” So Elijah rose and went down with him to the king. Elijah said to the king, “The LORD says this: You sent messengers to consult Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron. Did you do that because there is no God in Israel whose word you could seek? Because you did this, you will not come down from the bed you have gone up to; you will certainly die.” So Ahaziah died, in keeping with the word of the LORD that Elijah had spoken. Because Ahaziah had no son, Jehoram became king in his place, in the second year of Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah. The rest of the acts of Ahaziah, what he did, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel.

fields.title: 2 Kings 2
fields.body_html:
Elijah is taken up to heaven

When the LORD was about to take Elijah up to heaven by a whirlwind, Elijah and Elisha were setting out from Gilgal. Elijah said to Elisha, “Please stay here, because the LORD has sent me on to Bethel.” But Elisha said, “As surely as the LORD lives and as surely as you live, I will not leave you.” Then they went down together to Bethel. The company of prophets at Bethel came out to Elisha and asked him, “Do you know that the LORD is going to take your master from you today?” He said, “Yes, I know. Say no more.” Then Elijah said to him, “Elisha, please stay here, because the LORD has sent me to Jericho.” But he said, “As surely as the LORD lives and as surely as you live, I will not leave you.” So they came to Jericho. The company of prophets who were at Jericho came up to Elisha and said to him, “Do you know that the LORD is going to take your master from you today?” He answered, “Yes, I know. Say no more.” Then Elijah said to him, “Please stay here, because the LORD has sent me to the Jordan.” But he said, “As surely as the LORD lives and as surely as you live, I will not leave you.” And the two of them walked on. Fifty men of the company of prophets went along and stood some distance away, facing them, while the two of them stood beside the Jordan. Then Elijah took his cloak, rolled it up and struck the water. The water divided to one side and the other, and the two of them crossed over on dry ground. When they had crossed over, Elijah said to Elisha, “Before I am taken from you, tell me what I can do for you.” Elisha answered, “Please let me receive a double portion of your spirit.” Elijah said, “You have asked for something difficult. If you see me being taken from you, you will have it; if you do not, you will not.” As they were walking along and talking, suddenly a chariot of fire with horses of fire came between the two of them, and Elijah went up to heaven in the whirlwind. Elisha saw it, and he cried out, “My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!” And he did not see him again. Then he gripped his own garments and tore them in two. He picked up Elijah’s cloak, which had fallen from him, and went back and stood on the bank of the Jordan. He took Elijah’s cloak that had fallen from him, struck the water and said, “Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?” When he too had struck the water, it divided to one side and the other, and Elisha crossed over. When the company of prophets from Jericho, who were watching from the other side, saw him, they said, “The spirit of Elijah has come to rest on Elisha.” They went to meet him and bowed to the ground before him. They said to him, “Look, we your servants have fifty strong men with us. Please let them go and look for your master. It may be that the Spirit of the LORD has carried him off and set him down on some mountain or in some valley.” But he said, “Do not send them.” But they kept pressing him until he was embarrassed to refuse, so he said, “Send them.” They sent fifty men, and for three days they searched but did not find him. When they came back to him, he was staying at Jericho. He said to them, “Did I not tell you not to go?” The men of the city said to Elisha, “Look, my lord, as you can see, this city is in a good place, but the water is bad, and the land causes miscarriages.” He said, “Bring me a new bowl and put salt in it.” So they brought it to him. Then he went out to the spring and threw the salt into it, and said, “The LORD says this: ‘I have healed this water. From now on it will no longer cause death or miscarriage.’” So the water has been wholesome to this day, just as Elisha had said.

Elisha at Bethel

From there Elisha went up to Bethel. As he was going up the road, some young lads came out of the city and mocked him, saying, “Go on up, baldhead! Go on up, baldhead!” He turned around, looked at them, and cursed them in the name of the LORD. Then two female bears came out of the forest and savaged forty-two of the youngsters. From there he went on to Mount Carmel, and from there he went back to Samaria.

fields.title: 2 Kings 3
fields.body_html:
Jehoram king of Israel

In the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, Jehoram son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned twelve years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, though not like his father and mother. He removed the standing stone of Baal that his father had made. Yet he held on to the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, by which he led Israel to sin; he did not turn away from them.

War against Moab

Mesha king of Moab raised sheep, and he used to pay the king of Israel 100,000 lambs and the wool of 100,000 rams. But when Ahab died, the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel. So at that time King Jehoram marched out of Samaria and mustered all Israel. He also sent word to Jehoshaphat king of Judah. “The king of Moab,” he said, “has rebelled against me. Will you join me in battle against Moab?” Jehoshaphat answered, “I will go. I am as you are, my troops are as your troops, my horses as your horses.” Then he asked, “By which route shall we attack?” He answered, “By the road through the wilderness of Edom.” So the king of Israel set out with the king of Judah and the king of Edom. After a roundabout march of seven days, there was no water left for the army or for the animals that followed them. The king of Israel said, “How terrible! The LORD has called these three kings together to hand them over to Moab.” But Jehoshaphat asked, “Is there no prophet of the LORD here, through whom we can inquire of the LORD?” One of the king of Israel’s officials answered, “Elisha son of Shaphat is here, the man who used to pour water on Elijah’s hands.” Jehoshaphat said, “The word of the LORD is with him.” Then the king of Israel went down to him, with Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom. Elisha said to the king of Israel, “What do you and I have to do with each other? Go to your father’s prophets and your mother’s prophets.” But the king of Israel said to him, “No, for the LORD has called these three kings together to hand them over to Moab.” Elisha said, “As surely as the LORD of Armies lives, whom I serve, if I did not respect Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would not look at you or even notice you. But now bring me a musician.” While the musician was playing, the hand of the LORD came on Elisha. Then he said, “The LORD says this: ‘Dig ditch after ditch in this streambed.’ For the LORD says this: ‘You will see no wind and no rain, yet that streambed will fill with water, and you will drink, you and your livestock and your pack animals.’ This is only a small thing in the sight of the LORD; he will also hand Moab over to you. You will strike down every fortified town and every major town. You will cut down every good tree, block every spring of water, and ruin every good field with stones.” The next morning, about the time of the morning offering, water suddenly came flowing from the direction of Edom, and the land was filled with water. Meanwhile all Moab had heard that the kings had come to fight against them. Everyone old enough to put on a sword belt, and older, was called out, and they took up positions at the border. Early in the morning they got up, and the sun was shining on the water. To the Moabites facing it, the water looked as red as blood. They said, “This is blood! The kings must have fought one another and killed each other. Now, Moab, to the plunder!” But when the Moabites reached the camp of Israel, the Israelites sprang up and attacked them, and they fled. The Israelites pushed on into the land, striking down the Moabites. They tore down the towns, and each man threw a stone on every good field until it was covered. They blocked every spring of water and cut down every good tree. At last only Kir-hareseth was left with its stones standing, and the slingers surrounded it and attacked it. When the king of Moab saw that the battle was going against him, he took with him 700 swordsmen to try to break through to the king of Edom, but they failed. Then he took his firstborn son, who was to become king after him, and offered him as a burnt offering on the wall. And great wrath came against Israel, so they withdrew from him and returned to their own land.

fields.title: 2 Kings 4
fields.body_html:
The widow’s oil

The wife of a man from the company of prophets cried out to Elisha, “My husband, your servant, has died, and you know that your servant feared the LORD. Now the man he owed money to has come to take my two children as his slaves.” Elisha said to her, “What can I do for you? Tell me, what is there in your house?” She replied, “Your servant has nothing at all in the house, except a small jar of oil.” He said, “Go around and borrow containers from all your neighbors, empty ones, and not just a few. Then go inside with your sons and shut the door behind you. Pour oil into all these containers, and as each one is filled, set it aside.” So she left him and shut the door behind her and her sons. They kept bringing the containers to her, and she kept pouring. When the containers were all full, she told her son, “Bring me another one.” But he told her, “There are no more.” Then the oil stopped flowing. She came and told the man of God. He said, “Go and sell the oil, and pay off your debt. You and your sons can live on the rest.”

The woman of Shunem and her son

One day Elisha went on to Shunem. A wealthy woman lived there, and she pressed him to stay for a meal. After that, whenever he passed that way, he would stop there to eat. She said to her husband, “Listen, I am sure that this man who keeps coming our way is a holy man of God. Let us build a small room with walls on the roof and put a bed, a table, a chair and a lamp in it for him. Then whenever he comes to us, he can stay there.” One day Elisha came there, went into the upstairs room and lay down there. He said to his servant Gehazi, “Call the Shunammite woman.” So he called her, and she came and stood before him. Elisha said to Gehazi, “Tell her, ‘You have gone to all this trouble for us. What can be done for you? Can we speak for you to the king or to the commander of the army?’” She answered, “I live among my own people.” Elisha asked, “What then can be done for her?” Gehazi answered, “Well, she has no son, and her husband is old.” Elisha said, “Call her.” So Gehazi called her, and she stood in the doorway. Elisha said, “About this time next year you will be holding a son in your arms.” She said, “No, my lord, man of God! Do not deceive your servant.” But the woman conceived, and at that same season the following year she gave birth to a son, as Elisha had told her. The child grew. And one day he went out to join his father among the reapers. He said to his father, “My head! My head!” His father told a servant, “Carry him to his mother.” The servant picked him up and took him to his mother. He sat on her lap until noon, and then he died. She went upstairs and laid him on the bed of the man of God, shut the door on him, and went out. She called her husband and said, “Please send me a servant and one of the donkeys. I want to hurry to the man of God and come straight back.” He asked, “Why go to him today? It is neither a new moon nor a Sabbath.” “It is all right,” she said. She saddled the donkey and said to her servant, “Drive on and go! Do not slow down for my sake unless I tell you.” So she set off and came to the man of God at Mount Carmel. As soon as the man of God saw her in the distance, he said to Gehazi his servant, “Look, there is the Shunammite woman. Run now to meet her and ask her, ‘Are you all right? Is your husband all right? Is the child all right?’” She answered, “It is all right.” When she reached the man of God on the mountain, she clung to his feet. Gehazi came up to push her away, but the man of God said, “Let her be! She is in deep distress. the LORD has hidden it from me and not told me.” She said, “Did I ask my lord for a son? Did I not say, ‘Do not mislead me’?” Elisha said to Gehazi, “Tuck your robe into your belt, take my staff in your hand, and be on your way. If you meet anyone, do not greet them, and if anyone greets you, do not answer. Lay my staff on the boy’s face.” But the boy’s mother said, “As surely as the LORD lives and as surely as you live, I will not leave you.” So Elisha got up and followed her. Gehazi went ahead of them and put the staff on the boy’s face. But there was no sound and no response. So he came back to meet Elisha and reported, “The boy has not woken up.” When Elisha reached the house, there was the boy, dead, lying on his bed. He went in, shut the door on the two of them, and prayed to the LORD. Then he got up on the bed and lay on the child, putting his mouth on the child’s mouth, his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. As he stretched himself out over him, the boy’s body grew warm. Elisha got down and walked back and forth in the house, then went up and stretched himself out over him again. The boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes. Elisha called Gehazi and told him, “Call the Shunammite woman.” Gehazi called her, and when she came in, Elisha said, “Pick up your son.” She came in, fell at his feet, and bowed low to the ground. Then she lifted up her son and went out.

Death in the pot

Elisha went back to Gilgal while there was a famine in the land. When the company of prophets were sitting before him, he said to his servant, “Put the large pot on the fire and cook some stew for the company of prophets.” One of them went out into the fields to gather herbs. He found a wild vine and picked enough wild gourds from it to fill his cloak. He came back and sliced them into the pot of stew, though none of them knew what they were. They served it out for the men to eat. But as they were eating the stew, they cried out, “Man of God, there is death in the pot!” They were not able to eat it. Elisha said, “Then bring some flour.” He threw it into the pot and said, “Serve it to the people, and let them eat.” And there was nothing harmful in the pot.

Bread for a hundred men

A man came from Baal-shalishah, bringing the man of God bread from the firstfruits: twenty loaves of barley bread, and fresh ears of grain in his sack. Elisha said, “Give it to the people to eat.” His attendant said, “How can I set this in front of a hundred men?” But Elisha said, “Give it to the people to eat, for the LORD says this: ‘They will eat and have some left over.’” So he set it before them. They ate, and there was some left over, as the LORD had said.

fields.title: 2 Kings 5
fields.body_html:
Naaman is healed

Naaman was commander of the army of the king of Aram. His master regarded him as a great man and held him in high honor, because through him the LORD had given victory to Aram. He was a mighty warrior, but he had a serious skin disease. Raiding parties from Aram had gone out and had taken a young girl captive from the land of Israel, and she served Naaman’s wife. She said to her mistress, “If only my master could stand before the prophet in Samaria! Then he would free him from his skin disease.” Naaman went in and told his master, “This is what the girl from the land of Israel said.” The king of Aram said, “Go at once, and I will send a letter to the king of Israel.” So Naaman went, taking with him about 750 pounds of silver, about 150 pounds of gold and ten sets of fine clothes. He brought the letter to the king of Israel. It said, “With this letter I am sending my servant Naaman to you, so that you may cure him of his skin disease.” The king of Israel read the letter and at once tore his clothes. “Am I God,” he said, “to put to death and to give life, that this man sends someone to me to be cured of his skin disease? Think about it and see: he is looking for a reason to quarrel with me.” Elisha the man of God learned that the king of Israel had torn his clothes, and he sent this word to the king: “Why have you torn your clothes? Let the man come to me, and he will find out that Israel has a prophet.” So Naaman came with his horses and his chariot and stopped at the door of Elisha’s house. Elisha sent a messenger out to him to say, “Go and wash seven times in the Jordan. Your flesh will be restored, and you will be clean.” But Naaman went away angry. He said, “I thought that he would surely come out to me, stand and call on the name of the LORD his God, wave his hand over the spot and cure me of the disease. Are not the rivers of Damascus, Abana and Pharpar, better than any of the waters of Israel? Could I not wash in them and be made clean?” Then he turned and went off in a fury. His servants came up to him and said, “My father, had the prophet asked you to do something great, would you not have done it? How much more, then, should you obey when he tells you only, ‘Wash and be clean’!” So he went down and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, as the man of God had said. His flesh was restored and became like the flesh of a young boy, and he was clean. Then he went back to the man of God with all his company. He came and stood before him and said, “Now I know that in all the earth there is no God except in Israel. So now, please accept a gift from your servant.” But Elisha said, “As surely as the LORD lives, whom I serve, I will accept nothing.” Naaman pressed him to take it, but he refused. Then Naaman said, “If not, then please let your servant be given a load of earth, as much as a pair of mules can carry, because your servant will never again offer burnt offering or sacrifice to other gods, but only to the LORD. But in one matter may the LORD pardon your servant: when my master goes into the temple of Rimmon to bow down there, he leans on my arm, and I too bow down in the temple of Rimmon. When I bow down in the temple of Rimmon, may the LORD pardon your servant in this matter.” Elisha said to him, “Go in peace.” So Naaman left him and went some distance.

Gehazi’s greed

Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, said to himself, “My master has let this Aramean Naaman off without taking any of the things he brought. As surely as the LORD lives, I will chase after him and take something from him.” So Gehazi hurried after Naaman. When Naaman saw someone running after him, he got down from his chariot to meet him and asked, “Is everything all right?” He answered, “All is well. My master has sent me to say, ‘Two young men of the company of prophets have just arrived from the hill country of Ephraim. Please give them about 75 pounds of silver and two sets of clothes.’” Naaman said, “Please, take about 150 pounds.” He pressed Gehazi to take them, and tied up about 150 pounds of silver in two bags, with two sets of clothes. He gave them to two of his servants, and they carried them ahead of Gehazi. When Gehazi came to the hill, he took the things from them and put them away in the house. Then he sent the men off, and they left. Then he went in and stood before his master. Elisha asked him, “Where have you been, Gehazi?” He said, “Your servant has not gone anywhere.” But Elisha said to him, “Was not my heart there with you when a man turned from his chariot to meet you? Is this a time for taking money and taking clothes, olive groves and vineyards, sheep and cattle, male slaves and female slaves? So Naaman’s skin disease will cling to you and to your descendants forever.” And Gehazi went out from his presence with a serious skin disease, as white as snow.

fields.title: 2 Kings 6
fields.body_html:
The floating ax head

The company of prophets said to Elisha, “Look, the place where we live under your leadership is too small for us. Please let us go down to the Jordan. Each of us can take a log from there, and we can build ourselves a place to live there.” He said, “Go.” Then one of them said, “Please be willing to come with your servants.” “I will come,” he answered. So he went along with them. Once they reached the Jordan, they began cutting down trees. As one of them was felling a log, the axe head fell into the water. He cried out, “Oh no, my master! It was borrowed!” The man of God asked, “Where did it fall?” When the man showed him the place, Elisha cut off a stick, threw it in there, and made the iron float. “Pick it up,” he said. So the man reached out his hand and took it.

Elisha and the Aramean raiders

Now the king of Aram was at war with Israel. After consulting with his officials, he said, “I will set up my camp at such and such a place.” But the man of God sent this message to the king of Israel: “Take care not to pass by this place, because the Arameans are going down there.” So the king of Israel sent word to the place that the man of God had named to him. Time and again Elisha warned him, and the king was on his guard there, not once or twice only. This deeply troubled the king of Aram. He called his officials and said to them, “Will you not tell me which of us is on the side of the king of Israel?” One of his officials answered, “None of us, my lord the king. It is Elisha, the prophet in Israel. Even the words you speak in your bedroom, he reports to the king of Israel.” The king said, “Go and find out where he is, so that I can send men to seize him.” Word came back to him: “He is in Dothan.” So he sent horses and chariots there, a large force. They came by night and surrounded the city. When the servant of the man of God got up early in the morning and went out, there was an army with horses and chariots surrounding the city. His servant said to Elisha, “Oh no, my master! What shall we do?” “Do not be afraid,” Elisha answered. “There are more with us than there are with them.” Then Elisha prayed, “LORD, please open his eyes so that he can see.” The LORD opened the young man’s eyes, and he saw that the hill was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha. As the Arameans came down toward him, Elisha prayed to the LORD, “Please strike these people with a blinding light.” So he struck them with a blinding light, as Elisha had asked. Elisha said to them, “This is not the right road, and this is not the town. Come after me, and I will lead you to the man you are seeking.” So he brought them to Samaria. As soon as they entered Samaria, Elisha said, “LORD, open the eyes of these men so that they can see.” The LORD opened their eyes, and they looked and found that they were in the middle of Samaria. When the king of Israel saw them, he said to Elisha, “My father, shall I kill them? Shall I kill them?” “Do not kill them,” he answered. “Would you kill men you had captured with your own sword and bow? Set food and water before them, so that they can eat and drink and then go back to their master.” So the king prepared a great feast for them. When they had finished eating and drinking, he let them go, and they returned to their master. And the Aramean raiding bands did not come into the land of Israel again.

Famine in besieged Samaria

Some time after this, Ben-hadad king of Aram gathered his whole army, marched up, and laid siege to Samaria. There was a great famine in Samaria. The siege went on so long that a donkey’s head sold for about 2 pounds of silver, and about a cup of dove’s dung for about 2 ounces of silver. The king of Israel was passing by on the city wall when a woman called out to him, “Help, my lord the king!” He said, “If the LORD does not help you, where could I get help for you? From the threshing floor, or from the winepress?” Then the king asked her, “What is the matter?” She answered, “This woman said to me, ‘Give up your son, so that we can eat him today, and tomorrow we will eat my son.’ So we cooked my son and ate him. The next day I said to her, ‘Give up your son, so that we can eat him.’ But she has hidden her son.” When the king heard what the woman said, he tore his clothes. As he passed by on the wall, the people saw that he was wearing sackcloth underneath, against his skin. He said, “May God deal with me ever so severely if the head of Elisha son of Shaphat stays on his shoulders today!” Now Elisha was at home, with the elders sitting beside him. The king sent a man ahead of him, but before the messenger arrived, Elisha told the elders, “Do you see? This son of a murderer has sent someone to take off my head. Look, when the messenger comes, shut the door and hold it shut against him. Is not the sound of his master’s footsteps right behind him?” Elisha was still talking with them when the messenger came down to him. And he said, “This disaster comes from the LORD. Why should I go on waiting for the LORD?”

fields.title: 2 Kings 7
fields.body_html:
Elisha promises food

Elisha said, “Listen to the word of the LORD. The LORD says this: ‘About this time tomorrow, about 7 quarts of fine flour will sell for about 2/5 ounce of silver, and about 13 quarts of barley for about 2/5 ounce of silver, at the gate of Samaria.’” The officer whose arm the king leaned on replied to the man of God, “Even if the LORD were to make floodgates in the heavens, could this really happen?” Elisha replied, “With your own eyes you will see it happen, but you will not eat any of it.”

Four men find the camp deserted

Now there were four men with a serious skin disease at the entrance to the city gate. They said to one another, “Why are we sitting here waiting to die?” “If we say, ‘Let us go into the city,’ the famine is there, and we will die there. If we stay here, we will die. So come, let us go over to the Aramean camp and surrender. If they spare us, we will live; if they kill us, we will die.” So at dusk they got up and set out for the Aramean camp. But when they reached the edge of the camp, there was no one there at all. The Lord had made the Aramean army hear the sound of chariots and horses, the sound of a great army, and they said to one another, “Look, the king of Israel has hired the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Egypt to attack us!” So they got up and ran away at dusk, abandoning their tents, their horses and their donkeys. They left the camp just as it was and ran for their lives. When these men with the skin disease reached the edge of the camp, they went into one tent and ate and drank. They carried off silver, gold and clothing from it and went and hid them. Then they came back, went into another tent, carried off things from there too, and went and hid them. Then they said to one another, “What we are doing is not right. This is a day of good news, and we are keeping it to ourselves. If we wait until daylight, punishment will catch up with us. Come, let us go and report this to the king’s household.” So they came back and called out to the gatekeepers of the city and told them, “We went to the Aramean camp, and there was no one there, not a human voice to be heard. There were only horses tied up and donkeys tied up, and the tents left just as they were.” The gatekeepers shouted the news, and it was reported inside the king’s palace. The king got up in the night and said to his officials, “I will explain to you what the Arameans have done to us. They know that we are starving, and they have left their camp to hide out in the countryside. They are thinking, ‘When they come out of the city, we will capture them alive and get into the city.’” One of his officials answered, “Have some men take five of the horses still left in the city. Whatever happens to them, they are only like the rest of the people of Israel who are left here, like all the people of Israel who have already perished. Let us send them and see.” So they took two chariots with their horses, and the king sent them after the Aramean army with the order, “Go and find out.” They followed them as far as the Jordan, and the whole road was strewn with clothing and gear that the Arameans had flung away as they fled in haste. The messengers came back and reported to the king. Then the people went out and plundered the Aramean camp. So about 7 quarts of fine flour sold for about 2/5 ounce of silver, and about 13 quarts of barley for about 2/5 ounce of silver, just as the LORD had said. Now the king had put the officer on whose arm he leaned in charge of the gate. In the gateway the people trampled him, and he died, as the man of God had foretold when the king came down to him. For when the man of God told the king, “About 13 quarts of barley will sell for about 2/5 ounce of silver, and about 7 quarts of fine flour for about 2/5 ounce of silver, about this time tomorrow at the gate of Samaria,” the officer had answered the man of God, “Even if the LORD were to make floodgates in the heavens, could such a thing happen?” And Elisha had replied, “With your own eyes you will see it happen, but you will not eat any of it.” And that is exactly how it ended for him: in the gateway the people trampled him, and he died.

fields.title: 2 Kings 8
fields.body_html:
The Shunammite woman’s land restored

Elisha had said to the woman whose son he had brought back to life, “Get up and go away with your household, and stay wherever you can find a place to stay, for the LORD has called for a famine, and it will come on the land for seven years.” So the woman got up and did as the man of God had said. She went with her household and stayed in the land of the Philistines for seven years. At the end of the seven years, the woman came back from the land of the Philistines, and she went to appeal to the king for her house and her land. Now the king was speaking with Gehazi, the man of God’s servant, and said, “Please tell me about all the great things Elisha has done.” Just as he was telling the king how Elisha had brought the dead boy back to life, the woman whose son he had brought back to life came in, appealing to the king for her house and her land. Gehazi said, “My lord the king, here is the woman, and here is the son Elisha brought back to life!” The king asked the woman about it, and she told him. Then the king assigned an official to her case, with the order, “Give back everything that belonged to her, and all the produce of her field from the day she left the land until now.”

Elisha and Hazael

Elisha went to Damascus at a time when Ben-hadad king of Aram was sick. The king was told, “The man of God has come here.” The king said to Hazael, “Take a gift with you and go to meet the man of God. Ask the LORD through him, ‘Will I recover from this illness?’” So Hazael went to meet him, taking a gift with him, all kinds of fine goods from Damascus, forty camel loads. He came and stood before Elisha and said, “Your son Ben-hadad king of Aram sent me to ask you, ‘Will I recover from this illness?’” Elisha said to him, “Go and tell him, ‘You will certainly recover.’ But the LORD has shown me that he will certainly die.” Elisha fixed his gaze on Hazael and kept staring until Hazael was ashamed. Then the man of God wept. Hazael asked, “Why is my lord weeping?” He answered, “Because I know the harm you will do to the Israelites. You will set their fortresses on fire, kill their young men with the sword, dash their little children to pieces, and rip open their pregnant women.” Hazael said, “But what is your servant, a mere dog, that he should do such a great thing?” Elisha replied, “The LORD has shown me that you are to be king over Aram.” Then Hazael left Elisha and returned to his master. The king asked him, “What did Elisha say to you?” He replied, “He told me that you will certainly recover.” But the next day Hazael took the bed cloth, soaked it in water and spread it over the king’s face, and he died. And Hazael became king in his place.

Jehoram king of Judah

In the fifth year of Joram son of Ahab king of Israel, while Jehoshaphat was king of Judah, Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah became king. He was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem. He walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done, for he had married Ahab’s daughter. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. Yet the LORD was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of his servant David, since he had promised to give him a lamp for his descendants for all time. During his reign Edom rebelled against the rule of Judah and set up a king of its own. So Joram crossed over to Zair with all his chariots. He rose by night and attacked the Edomites who had surrounded him and the chariot commanders, and the troops fled to their homes. So Edom has been in rebellion against the rule of Judah to this day. Libnah also rebelled at that same time. The rest of the acts of Joram and all that he did are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Judah. Then Joram rested with his ancestors and was buried with them in the City of David. His son Ahaziah became king in his place.

Ahaziah king of Judah

In the twelfth year of Joram son of Ahab king of Israel, Ahaziah son of Jehoram king of Judah became king. Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Athaliah, the granddaughter of Omri king of Israel. He walked in the way of the house of Ahab and did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as the house of Ahab had done, for he was related by marriage to the house of Ahab. He went with Joram son of Ahab to war against Hazael king of Aram at Ramoth-gilead, and Joram was wounded by the Arameans. King Joram went back to Jezreel to recover from the wounds the Arameans had given him at Ramah, in his battle with Hazael king of Aram. Ahaziah son of Jehoram king of Judah then went down to see Joram son of Ahab in Jezreel, because he was wounded.

fields.title: 2 Kings 9
fields.body_html:
Jehu is anointed king

Elisha the prophet called one of the company of prophets and said to him, “Tuck your robe into your belt, take this flask of oil with you, and go to Ramoth-gilead. When you get there, look for Jehu son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi. Go in, have him get up from among his fellow officers, and take him into an inner room. Then pour the flask of oil over his head and say, ‘The LORD says this: I anoint you king over Israel.’ After that, open the door and run; do not wait.” So the young man, the prophet’s servant, went to Ramoth-gilead. When he arrived, the commanders of the army were sitting together. He said, “I have a message for you, commander.” Jehu asked, “For which one of us?” He answered, “For you, commander.” Jehu got up and went into the house. The young man poured the oil on his head and said to him, “The LORD, the God of Israel, says this: I anoint you king over the people of the LORD, over Israel. You are to strike down the house of your master Ahab, and so I will avenge on Jezebel the blood of my servants the prophets, and of all who serve the LORD. The whole house of Ahab will perish. From Ahab I will cut off every male in Israel, whether bond or free. I will make the house of Ahab like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat and like the house of Baasha son of Ahijah. As for Jezebel, the dogs will eat her on the plot of ground at Jezreel, and no one will bury her.” Then he opened the door and ran. When Jehu came out to his master’s officers, one of them asked him, “Is all well? Why did this madman come to you?” He told them, “You know the man and the way he talks.” But they said, “That is not true! Tell us.” So he said, “This is what he told me: ‘The LORD says this: I anoint you king over Israel.’” At once each man took off his cloak and spread it under Jehu on the bare steps. They blew the ram’s horn and shouted, “Jehu is king!” So Jehu son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi plotted against Joram. Joram and all Israel had been holding Ramoth-gilead against Hazael king of Aram, but King Jehoram had gone back to Jezreel to recover from the wounds the Arameans had given him when he fought Hazael king of Aram. Jehu said, “If you are with me, do not let anyone slip out of the city to go and tell the news in Jezreel.” Then Jehu got into his chariot and set out for Jezreel, because Joram was lying ill there, and Ahaziah king of Judah had come down to visit Joram. The watchman standing on the tower in Jezreel saw Jehu’s troop coming, and he said, “I see a troop of men.” Jehoram said, “Get a horseman and send him to meet them, and have him ask, ‘Is it peace?’” So the horseman went to meet Jehu and said, “The king says this: ‘Is it peace?’” Jehu said, “What business of yours is peace? Fall in behind me.” The watchman reported, “The messenger has reached them, but he is not coming back.” Then Joram sent a second horseman. He came to them and said, “The king says this: ‘Is it peace?’” Jehu said, “What business of yours is peace? Fall in behind me.” The watchman reported again, “He reached them, but he is not coming back either. And the driving is like the driving of Jehu son of Nimshi, for he drives like a madman.” Jehoram said, “Hitch up my chariot!” When his chariot was ready, Jehoram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah rode out, each in his own chariot, to meet Jehu, and they met him on the plot of ground that had belonged to Naboth the Jezreelite. When Jehoram saw Jehu, he said, “Is it peace, Jehu?” Jehu answered, “How can there be peace, as long as the prostitutions and the many sorceries of your mother Jezebel go on?” Jehoram turned his chariot around and fled, calling out to Ahaziah, “Treachery, Ahaziah!” Jehu drew his bow with all his strength and shot Jehoram between the shoulders. The arrow went through his heart, and he slumped down in his chariot. Jehu said to his officer Bidkar, “Pick him up and throw him on the plot of ground that was Naboth the Jezreelite’s field. Remember how you and I were riding side by side behind his father Ahab, when the LORD spoke this oracle against him: ‘I surely saw the blood of Naboth and of his sons yesterday, declares the LORD, and I will repay you on this plot of ground, declares the LORD.’ So now pick him up and throw him on that plot of ground, as the LORD said.” When Ahaziah king of Judah saw this, he fled along the road to Beth-haggan. Jehu chased him and said, “Shoot him too!” They shot him in his chariot on the way up to Gur, near Ibleam, but he escaped to Megiddo and died there. His officials took him to Jerusalem in a chariot and buried him with his ancestors in his tomb in the City of David.

The death of Jezebel

Ahaziah had become king over Judah in the eleventh year of Joram son of Ahab. Then Jehu came to Jezreel. When Jezebel heard of it, she painted her eyes, arranged her hair and looked down from the window. As Jehu came in through the gate, she said, “Is it peace, you Zimri, murderer of your master?” Jehu looked up at the window. “Who is on my side?” he called. “Who?” Two or three officials looked down at him. “Throw her down!” he said. They threw her down, and some of her blood spattered on the wall and on the horses, and Jehu drove over her. Then Jehu went in and ate and drank. He said, “See to this cursed woman and bury her, for she was a king’s daughter.” But when they went to bury her, they found nothing of her except her skull, her feet and the palms of her hands. They went back and told Jehu, and he said, “This is the word of the LORD that he spoke through his servant Elijah the Tishbite: ‘The dogs will eat the flesh of Jezebel on the plot of ground at Jezreel, and the corpse of Jezebel will be like dung on the surface of the field in the plot of ground at Jezreel, so that no one will be able to say, “This is Jezebel.”‘”

fields.title: 2 Kings 10
fields.body_html:
The end of Ahab’s family

There were seventy sons of Ahab in Samaria. Jehu wrote letters and sent them there, to the officials of Jezreel, the elders, and those who were guardians of Ahab’s sons. The letters said: “Now, the moment this letter reaches you, since you have your master’s sons with you, along with chariots and horses, a fortified city and weapons, pick the best and most fitting of your master’s sons, put him on his father’s throne, and fight for the house of your master.” But they were terrified and said, “Look, the two kings could not stand against him. How can we?” So the palace steward, the governor of the city, the elders and the guardians sent word to Jehu: “We are your servants, and we will do everything you tell us. We will not make anyone king. Do whatever you think best.” Then he wrote them a second letter: “If you are on my side and will obey me, take the heads of the men, your master’s sons, and be with me in Jezreel by this time tomorrow.” Now the king’s sons, seventy of them, were with the leading men of the city, who were bringing them up. When the letter came to them, they took the king’s sons, seventy men, and slaughtered them. Then they put the heads in baskets and sent them to Jehu in Jezreel. The messenger came and reported to Jehu, “They have brought the heads of the king’s sons.” Jehu said, “Pile them in two heaps at the entrance of the city gate until morning.” In the morning he went out, stood there and said to all the people, “You are innocent. It was I who plotted against my master and killed him. But who struck down all these? Know, then, that not one word that the LORD spoke against the house of Ahab will fail. The LORD has done what he said through his servant Elijah.” So Jehu struck down everyone who was left of Ahab’s house in Jezreel, along with all his leading men, his close friends and his priests, until he left him no survivor. Then Jehu set out and went to Samaria. On the way, when he was at Beth-eked of the Shepherds, Jehu met relatives of Ahaziah king of Judah. “Who are you?” he asked. They answered, “We are Ahaziah’s relatives. We have come down to greet the king’s sons and the queen mother’s sons.” Jehu said, “Take them alive!” So they took them alive and slaughtered them at the pit of Beth-eked, forty-two men. He did not spare a single one of them.

Leaving there, he came upon Jehonadab son of Rechab, who was on his way to meet him. Jehu greeted him and said to him, “Is your heart right with mine, as my heart is with yours?” Jehonadab replied, “It is.” “If so,” said Jehu, “give me your hand.” He gave him his hand, and Jehu took him up into the chariot beside him. He said, “Come with me and see how zealous I am for the LORD.” So they had him ride in Jehu’s chariot. When he came to Samaria, he struck down everyone who was left of Ahab’s family in Samaria, until he had wiped them out, as the LORD had said through Elijah.

Jehu destroys Baal worship

Then Jehu gathered all the people and said to them, “Ahab served Baal a little. Jehu will serve him much more. Now summon to me all the prophets of Baal, all his worshipers and all his priests. Let no one be missing, for I am holding a great sacrifice for Baal. Anyone who is missing will not live.” But Jehu was acting with cunning, so that he could destroy the worshipers of Baal. Jehu said, “Set apart a solemn assembly for Baal.” So they announced it. Jehu sent word through all Israel, and all the worshipers of Baal came. Not one was left who did not come. They went into the temple of Baal, and the temple of Baal was filled from one end to the other. Jehu told the keeper of the wardrobe, “Bring out robes for every worshiper of Baal.” And he brought robes out for them. Then Jehu went into the temple of Baal with Jehonadab son of Rechab. He said to the worshipers of Baal, “Search and make sure that none of the servants of the LORD are here with you, but only the worshipers of Baal.” The worshipers went in to make sacrifices and burnt offerings. Jehu had already posted eighty men outside and had warned them, “If any of the men I am bringing into your hands escapes, the one who let him go will pay with his life.” The moment he had finished offering the burnt offering, Jehu ordered the guards and the officers, “Go in and kill them. Do not let anyone get out.” So they killed them with the sword. The guards and the officers threw the bodies out and then went into the inner shrine of the temple of Baal. They brought out the standing stones of the temple of Baal and burned them. They demolished the standing stone of Baal and tore down the temple of Baal, and they made it a latrine, as it is to this day. So Jehu wiped out Baal worship from Israel. But Jehu did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, by which he led Israel to sin: the golden calves at Bethel and at Dan.

The rest of Jehu’s reign

Then the LORD told Jehu, “You have done well in doing what is right in my sight. Because you have dealt with the house of Ahab in keeping with all that was in my heart, your sons to the fourth generation will sit on the throne of Israel.” Yet Jehu took no care to walk in the law of the LORD, the God of Israel, with his whole heart. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam, by which he led Israel to sin. In those days the LORD began to cut away parts of Israel. Hazael defeated the Israelites throughout their territory, from the Jordan eastward: all the land of Gilead, the land of the Gadites, the Reubenites and the Manassites, from Aroer by the Arnon Valley, both Gilead and Bashan. The rest of the acts of Jehu, all that he did and all his might, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel. Jehu rested with his ancestors and was buried in Samaria, and his son Jehoahaz became king in his place. Jehu reigned over Israel in Samaria for twenty-eight years.

fields.title: 2 Kings 11
fields.body_html:
Athaliah seizes the throne

Athaliah, Ahaziah’s mother, saw that her son was dead, and she set out to destroy the whole royal family. But Jehosheba, King Joram’s daughter and Ahaziah’s sister, took Ahaziah’s son Joash and secretly took him out from among the king’s sons who were about to be killed. She put him and his nurse in the bedroom, and they hid him from Athaliah, so he was not killed. He stayed hidden with her in the house of the LORD six years, during Athaliah’s rule over the land.

Joash is crowned

In the seventh year Jehoiada sent for the commanders of hundreds of the Carites and of the guards and had them brought to him in the house of the LORD. He made a covenant with them and put them under oath in the house of the LORD. Then he showed them the king’s son. He gave them this order: “Here is what you must do. One third of you, the men who come on duty on the sabbath, will keep watch over the king’s palace, one third at the Sur Gate, and one third at the gate behind the guards. So you will guard the palace in turns. The two companies of you who go off duty on the sabbath are all to keep watch over the house of the LORD to protect the king. Surround the king on every side, each man with his weapons in hand. Anyone who comes within your ranks must be put to death. Stay with the king wherever he goes.” The commanders of hundreds did everything Jehoiada the priest had ordered. Each brought his men, both the ones who came on duty on the sabbath and the ones who went off duty that day, and they came to Jehoiada the priest. The priest gave the commanders of hundreds the spears and shields that had belonged to King David and were kept in the house of the LORD. The guards took their places, each man with his weapons in hand, from the south side of the temple to the north side, beside the altar and the temple, surrounding the king. Then Jehoiada brought out the king’s son and put on him the crown and the testimony. They made him king and anointed him. Then they clapped their hands and shouted, “Long live the king!”

When Athaliah heard the noise of the guards and the people, she went to the people at the house of the LORD. She looked, and there was the king, standing by the pillar as the custom was, with the commanders and the trumpeters beside him. All the people of the land were rejoicing and blowing trumpets. Athaliah tore her clothes and cried out, “Treason! Treason!”

Jehoiada the priest gave orders to the commanders of hundreds who were in charge of the troops: “Bring her out between the ranks, and kill with the sword anyone who follows her.” For the priest had said, “Do not let her be killed in the house of the LORD.” They seized her, and she went out by way of the horses’ entrance to the king’s palace, and there she was put to death.

Jehoiada’s covenant and Athaliah’s end

Jehoiada made the covenant between the LORD, the king and the people, that they would be the people of the LORD. He also made one between the king and the people. Then all the people of the land went to Baal’s house and tore it down. They smashed its altars and its images to pieces, and killed Mattan, Baal’s priest, before the altars. The priest posted guards over the house of the LORD. He took the commanders of hundreds, the Carites, the guards and all the people of the land. They escorted the king down from the house of the LORD and went by way of the gate of the guards to the king’s palace. And the king took his seat on the royal throne. All the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was at peace. Athaliah had been put to death with the sword at the king’s palace.

Jehoash was seven years old when he became king.

fields.title: 2 Kings 12
fields.body_html:
Jehoash king of Judah

In the seventh year of Jehu, Jehoash became king, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Zibiah from Beersheba. Jehoash did what was right in the sight of the LORD all his days, because Jehoiada the priest instructed him. The high places, however, were not removed. The people still offered sacrifices and burned incense at the high places. Jehoash said to the priests, “All the money from the holy gifts that is brought into the house of the LORD, the money of those who are counted, the money for persons at the value set for each, and all the money anyone is moved to bring into the house of the LORD, let the priests take it, each from the people he knows, and let them repair the damage to the house wherever any damage is found.”

Repairs to the temple

But by the twenty-third year of King Jehoash, the priests still had not repaired the damage to the house. So King Jehoash summoned Jehoiada the priest and the other priests and said to them, “Why are you not repairing the damage to the house? From now on take no more money from the people you know. Hand it over for the damage to the house.” The priests agreed that they would take no more money from the people and would not be the ones to repair the damage to the house. Then Jehoiada the priest took a chest and drilled a hole in its lid. He placed it next to the altar, on the right side as people enter the house of the LORD. The priests who guarded the doorway put into it all the money brought into the house of the LORD. Each time they saw that the chest held a large sum, the king’s secretary and the high priest came up. They tied up in bags the money found in the house of the LORD and counted it. Then they gave the weighed money to the men doing the work, who had been put in charge of the house of the LORD. These paid it out to the carpenters and the builders who were working on the house of the LORD, and to the masons and the stonecutters. With it they also bought timber and dressed stone for mending the house of the LORD, and paid every other cost of the repairs. But none of the money brought into the house of the LORD was used to make silver basins, wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, trumpets, or any other articles of gold or silver for the house of the LORD, for it was given to the men doing the work, who used it to repair the house of the LORD. No accounting was asked of the men who were handed the money to pay the workmen, because those men dealt honestly. The money from guilt offerings and from sin offerings did not go into the house of the LORD. It was for the priests.

Hazael threatens Jerusalem

At that time Hazael king of Aram went up and fought against Gath and captured it. Then Hazael turned to go up against Jerusalem. So Jehoash king of Judah took all the holy gifts that his ancestors Jehoshaphat, Jehoram and Ahaziah, kings of Judah, had dedicated, along with his own holy gifts and all the gold there was in the treasuries of the house of the LORD and of the king’s palace, and sent them to Hazael king of Aram. Then Hazael withdrew from Jerusalem. The rest of the acts of Joash, and all that he did, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Judah. His officials rose up and formed a conspiracy, and they struck down Joash at Beth-millo, on the road that goes down to Silla. It was his officials Jozabad son of Shimeath and Jehozabad son of Shomer who struck him down, and he died. He was buried with his ancestors in the City of David, and his son Amaziah became king in his place.

fields.title: 2 Kings 13
fields.body_html:
Jehoahaz king of Israel

In the twenty-third year of Joash son of Ahaziah king of Judah, Jehoahaz son of Jehu became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned seventeen years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and followed the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, by which he led Israel to sin; he did not turn away from them. So the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and he gave them into the power of Hazael king of Aram and of Ben-hadad son of Hazael throughout that time. Then Jehoahaz pleaded with the LORD for favor, and the LORD listened to him, because he saw how the king of Aram was oppressing Israel. The LORD gave Israel a deliverer, and they escaped from the power of Aram. So the Israelites lived in their homes as they had before. Yet they did not turn away from the sins of the house of Jeroboam, by which he led Israel to sin, but kept walking in them. The Asherah pole also remained standing in Samaria. Jehoahaz had been left with no troops except fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and 10,000 foot soldiers, because the king of Aram had wiped them out and made them like dust to be trampled. The rest of the acts of Jehoahaz, all that he did and his might, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel. Jehoahaz rested with his ancestors, and they buried him in Samaria. His son Joash became king in his place.

Jehoash king of Israel

In the thirty-seventh year of Joash king of Judah, Jehoash son of Jehoahaz became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned sixteen years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not turn away from any of the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, by which he led Israel to sin, but walked in them. The rest of the acts of Joash, all that he did and the might with which he fought against Amaziah king of Judah, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel. Joash rested with his ancestors, and Jeroboam sat on his throne. Joash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel.

Elisha’s last prophecy

Now Elisha had fallen ill with the sickness that would bring his death. Joash king of Israel went down to see him and wept over him. He said, “My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!” Elisha said to him, “Take a bow and arrows.” So he took a bow and arrows. Then he said to the king of Israel, “Put your hand to the bow.” He did so, and Elisha laid his hands on the king’s hands. He said, “Open the window toward the east,” and he opened it. Elisha said, “Shoot!” and he shot. Then Elisha said, “The LORD’s arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Aram! You will strike down Aram at Aphek until you have made an end of it.” “Take the arrows,” he said, and the king took them. Then he told the king of Israel, “Strike the ground.” He struck it three times and stopped. The man of God was angry with him. “You ought to have struck five or six times!” he said. “Then you would have struck Aram down until it was finished. As it is, you will strike Aram down only three times.”

Elisha died, and they buried him. Now raiding bands from Moab used to come into the land each spring. Once, as some people were burying a man, suddenly they saw a raiding band, and they threw the man into Elisha’s grave. When the man touched Elisha’s bones, he came to life and stood up on his feet.

Israel wins back its towns

Hazael king of Aram oppressed Israel throughout the reign of Jehoahaz. But the LORD was gracious to them and had compassion on them. He turned toward them for the sake of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He was not willing to destroy them, and he had not yet cast them out of his presence. When Hazael king of Aram died, his son Ben-hadad became king in his place. Then Jehoash son of Jehoahaz recaptured from Ben-hadad son of Hazael the cities that Ben-hadad had taken in war from his father Jehoahaz. Three times Joash struck him down, and he recovered the cities of Israel.

fields.title: 2 Kings 14
fields.body_html:
Amaziah king of Judah

In the second year of Joash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel, Amaziah son of Joash became king of Judah. He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jehoaddin; she was from Jerusalem. He did what was right in the sight of the LORD, yet not as his ancestor David had done. He did everything just as his father Joash had done. Yet the high places were not taken away; the people still offered sacrifices and burned incense at the high places.
