As soon as the kingdom was firmly in his control, he executed the officials who had murdered his father the king. But he did not put to death the children of the murderers. In this he kept to the book of the law of Moses, in which the LORD commanded, “Parents are not to be put to death for their children, nor children for their parents. Each one is to be put to death only for their own sin.” He defeated the Edomites in the Valley of Salt, 10,000 of them, and captured Sela in battle. He named it Joktheel, and it is called that to this day.

Amaziah challenges Jehoash

Then Amaziah sent messengers to Jehoash son of Jehoahaz son of Jehu, king of Israel, to say, “Come, let us meet face to face.” Jehoash king of Israel sent back word to Amaziah king of Judah: “There was a thistle in Lebanon that sent word to a cedar in Lebanon: ‘Give your daughter to my son as his wife.’ Then a wild animal in Lebanon came by and trampled the thistle. You have certainly defeated Edom, and now your heart has made you proud. Enjoy your glory, but stay at home. Why stir up trouble that will only bring you down, you and Judah with you?” Amaziah, however, would not listen. So Jehoash king of Israel went up against him, and the two kings, he and Amaziah king of Judah, met face to face at Beth-shemesh, which belongs to Judah. Judah was defeated by Israel, and every man fled to his home. Jehoash king of Israel took Amaziah king of Judah prisoner at Beth-shemesh; Amaziah was the son of Jehoash son of Ahaziah. Then Jehoash came to Jerusalem and tore down the wall of Jerusalem along a stretch of about 600 feet, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate. He carried off all the gold and silver, and every article that was found in the house of the LORD and in the palace treasuries. He also took hostages, and then he returned to Samaria. The rest of the acts of Jehoash, what he did, his might and how he fought against Amaziah king of Judah, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel. Then Jehoash rested with his ancestors and was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel. His son Jeroboam became king in his place.

Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah lived fifteen years after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel. The rest of the acts of Amaziah are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Judah. Some in Jerusalem formed a conspiracy against him, and he fled to Lachish. But they sent men after him to Lachish and put him to death there. They brought his body back on horses, and he was buried in Jerusalem with his ancestors in the City of David. Then all the people of Judah took Azariah, then sixteen years old, and made him king to succeed his father Amaziah. It was he who rebuilt Elath and won it back for Judah, after King Amaziah had rested with his ancestors.

Jeroboam king of Israel

In the fifteenth year of Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah, Jeroboam son of Joash became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned forty-one years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not turn away from any of the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel to sin. He restored the border of Israel from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah, by the word of the LORD the God of Israel, which he had spoken through his servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher. For the LORD saw that Israel’s suffering was very bitter. No one was left, bound or free, and there was no one to help Israel. The LORD had not said that he would blot out the name of Israel from under the heavens, so he saved them through Jeroboam son of Joash. The rest of the acts of Jeroboam, all that he did, his might, how he fought, and how he won back for Israel Damascus and Hamath, which had belonged to Judah, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel. Then Jeroboam rested with his ancestors, the kings of Israel. His son Zechariah became king in his place.

fields.title: 2 Kings 15
fields.body_html:
Azariah king of Judah

In the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Azariah son of Amaziah king of Judah became king. He was sixteen years old when he became king, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jecoliah; she was from Jerusalem. He did what was right in the sight of the LORD, just as his father Amaziah had done. However, the high places were not removed; the people still offered sacrifices and burned incense at the high places. The LORD struck the king, and he had a serious skin disease until the day he died. He lived in a separate house, while Jotham the king’s son was in charge of the palace and governed the people of the land. The rest of the acts of Azariah, and all that he did, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Judah. Then Azariah rested with his ancestors and was buried with them in the City of David. His son Jotham became king in his place.

Zechariah king of Israel

In the thirty-eighth year of Azariah king of Judah, Zechariah son of Jeroboam became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned six months. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as his ancestors had done. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel to sin. Shallum son of Jabesh plotted against him. He struck him down in front of the people, killed him and became king in his place. The rest of the acts of Zechariah are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel. This was the word of the LORD that he had spoken to Jehu: “Your sons will sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation.” And so it happened.

Shallum king of Israel

Shallum son of Jabesh became king in the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah king of Judah, and he reigned one full month in Samaria. Then Menahem son of Gadi went up from Tirzah and came to Samaria. He struck down Shallum son of Jabesh in Samaria, killed him and became king in his place. The rest of the acts of Shallum, and the conspiracy he carried out, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel.

At that time Menahem attacked Tiphsah and everyone in it and its territory, starting from Tirzah, because they would not open the gates to him. He struck it down, and he ripped open all its pregnant women.

Menahem king of Israel

In the thirty-ninth year of Azariah king of Judah, Menahem son of Gadi became king over Israel, and he reigned ten years in Samaria. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. All his life he did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel to sin. Pul king of Assyria came against the land, and Menahem gave Pul about 37 tons of silver so that he would support him and strengthen his hold on the kingdom. Menahem raised the silver from Israel, from all the wealthy men, to give to the king of Assyria: about 1 1/4 pounds of silver from each man. So the king of Assyria turned back and did not stay there in the land. The rest of the acts of Menahem, and all that he did, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel. Then Menahem rested with his ancestors, and his son Pekahiah became king in his place.

Pekahiah king of Israel

In the fiftieth year of Azariah king of Judah, Pekahiah son of Menahem became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned two years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel to sin. Pekah son of Remaliah, his officer, plotted against him. He struck him down in Samaria, in the citadel of the royal palace, along with Argob and Arieh. Fifty men of Gilead were with Pekah. He killed Pekahiah and became king in his place. The rest of the acts of Pekahiah, and all that he did, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel.

Pekah king of Israel

In the fifty-second year of Azariah king of Judah, Pekah son of Remaliah became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned twenty years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel to sin. During the reign of Pekah king of Israel, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came. He captured Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh and Hazor, as well as Gilead and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali. He took the people away into exile in Assyria. Then Hoshea son of Elah formed a conspiracy against Pekah son of Remaliah. He struck him down, killed him and became king in his place, in the twentieth year of Jotham son of Uzziah. The rest of the acts of Pekah, and all that he did, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel.

Jotham king of Judah

In the second year of Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel, Jotham son of Uzziah king of Judah became king. He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jerusha daughter of Zadok. He did what was right in the sight of the LORD, just as his father Uzziah had done. However, the high places were not removed; the people still offered sacrifices and burned incense at the high places. He built the Upper Gate of the house of the LORD. The rest of the acts of Jotham, what he did, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Judah. In those days the LORD began sending Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah against Judah. Then Jotham rested with his ancestors and was buried with them in the City of his ancestor David. His son Ahaz became king in his place.

fields.title: 2 Kings 16
fields.body_html:
Ahaz king of Judah

In the seventeenth year of Pekah son of Remaliah, Ahaz son of Jotham became king of Judah. Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. He did not do what was right in the sight of the LORD his God, as his ancestor David had done. He walked in the way of the kings of Israel. He even made his son pass through the fire, following the detestable practices of the nations that the LORD had driven out ahead of the Israelites. He offered sacrifices and burned incense at the high places, on the hills and under every leafy tree. Then Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, came up to Jerusalem to make war. They besieged Ahaz, but they were not able to take the city. At that time Rezin king of Aram recovered Elath for Aram and drove the people of Judah out of Elath. Edomites came to Elath, and they have lived there to this day.

Ahaz turns to Assyria

Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria with this message: “I am your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me from the power of the king of Aram and the king of Israel, who are attacking me.” Ahaz took the silver and gold to be found in the house of the LORD and in the palace treasuries, and he sent it as a bribe to the king of Assyria. The king of Assyria agreed to his request. He marched up against Damascus and captured it. He took its people into exile to Kir and put Rezin to death. King Ahaz went to meet Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria at Damascus. There he saw the altar that stood in Damascus. Then King Ahaz sent Uriah the priest a model and a design of the altar, with all the details of how it was made. Uriah the priest built the altar following everything King Ahaz had sent from Damascus. He had it finished by the time King Ahaz came back from Damascus. On his return from Damascus the king saw the altar; he approached it and offered sacrifices on it. He burned his burnt offering and grain offering, poured his drink offering, and splashed the blood of his peace offerings on the altar. As for the bronze altar that stood before the LORD, he moved it from the front of the temple, from its place between the new altar and the house of the LORD, and set it beside the new altar on the north. Then King Ahaz gave orders to Uriah the priest: “On the great altar burn the morning burnt offering and the evening grain offering, the king’s burnt offering and his grain offering, and the burnt offering of all the people of the land with their grain offerings and drink offerings. Splash on it all the blood of the burnt offerings and of the sacrifices. But the bronze altar will be for me to seek guidance by.” Uriah the priest did everything King Ahaz commanded. King Ahaz cut off the panels of the stands and removed the basins from them. He took the Sea down from the bronze oxen that held it up and set it on a stone pavement. He also removed from the house of the LORD the covered place for the Sabbath that had been built at the temple, and the king’s outer entrance. He did this because of the king of Assyria. The rest of the acts of Ahaz, what he did, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Judah. Then Ahaz rested with his ancestors and was buried with them in the City of David. His son Hezekiah became king in his place.

fields.title: 2 Kings 17
fields.body_html:
Hoshea, the last king of Israel

In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah, Hoshea son of Elah became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned nine years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, yet not as the kings of Israel before him had done. Shalmaneser king of Assyria marched against him, and Hoshea became his vassal and paid him tribute. But the king of Assyria found Hoshea plotting against him, for he had sent envoys to So king of Egypt and had not paid the king of Assyria his tribute as in other years. So the king of Assyria arrested him and held him bound in prison. Then the king of Assyria invaded the whole land. He went up to Samaria and laid siege to it for three years. In Hoshea’s ninth year the king of Assyria captured Samaria and carried the Israelites away into exile to Assyria. He settled them in Halah, on the Habor, Gozan’s river, and in the cities of the Medes.

Why Israel went into exile

This happened because the Israelites had sinned against the LORD their God, who had brought them up from the land of Egypt and out from under the power of Pharaoh king of Egypt. They had feared other gods. They walked in the statutes of the nations whom the LORD had driven out before the Israelites, and in the statutes that the kings of Israel had made. In secret the Israelites did things against the LORD their God that were not right. They built high places for themselves in all their towns, from the watchtower to the fortified city. They set up standing stones and Asherah poles for themselves on every high hill and under every leafy tree. There on all the high places they burned incense, as the nations had done whom the LORD carried away before them, and they did evil things that provoked the LORD to anger. They served the idols, though the LORD had told them, “You must not do this.” Yet the LORD warned Israel and Judah through every prophet and every seer: “Turn back from your evil ways. Keep my commandments and my statutes, in keeping with the whole law that I commanded your ancestors and sent to you through my servants the prophets.” But they would not listen. They stiffened their necks as their ancestors had done, who did not trust in the LORD their God. They rejected his statutes, the covenant he had made with their ancestors, and the decrees by which he had warned them. They went after worthless idols and became worthless themselves. They followed the nations around them, although the LORD had commanded them not to do as those nations did. They abandoned every commandment of the LORD their God and made themselves cast images, two calves. They made an Asherah pole, bowed down to all the host of heaven, and served Baal. They made their sons and daughters pass through the fire, practiced divination and read omens, and sold themselves to do what was evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger. So the LORD was very angry with Israel and removed them from his presence. None was left but the tribe of Judah alone. Even Judah failed to keep the commandments of the LORD their God. They walked in the statutes that Israel had made. So the LORD rejected all Israel’s descendants. He afflicted them and handed them over to plunderers, until he had thrown them out of his presence. When he had torn Israel from David’s house, they made Jeroboam son of Nebat king. Jeroboam drove Israel away from following the LORD and led them to commit a great sin. The Israelites walked in all the sins that Jeroboam committed and did not turn away from them, until the LORD removed Israel from his presence, as he had said through all his servants the prophets. So Israel went into exile from its own land to Assyria, to this day.

New settlers in Samaria

From Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath and Sepharvaim the king of Assyria brought people and settled them in the cities of Samaria in place of the Israelites. They took possession of Samaria and lived in its cities. When they first lived there they did not fear the LORD, so the LORD sent lions among them, and the lions killed some of them. Word was brought to the king of Assyria: “The nations you carried away and settled in the cities of Samaria do not know the custom of the god of the land. So he has sent lions among them, and they are killing them, because they do not know what the god of the land requires.” Then the king of Assyria gave orders: “Send back there one of the priests you carried away from there. Let him go and live there and teach them the custom of the god of the land.” So one of the priests who had been carried away from Samaria came and lived in Bethel, and he taught them how they should fear the LORD. But each nation made its own gods and set them up in the shrines of the high places that the people of Samaria had made, each nation in the cities where it lived. The people of Babylon made Succoth-benoth, the people of Cuth made Nergal, and the people of Hamath made Ashima. The Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak, while the Sepharvites burned their children in the fire for Adrammelech and Anammelech, gods of Sepharvaim. They feared the LORD, but they also appointed priests of the high places from all sorts of their own people, who offered sacrifices for them in the shrines of the high places. They feared the LORD, and they served their own gods, according to the custom of the nations from which they had been carried away. To this day they keep to their former customs. They do not truly fear the LORD, and they do not follow their statutes and rulings, or the law and the commandment that the LORD gave the descendants of Jacob, the man he named Israel. The LORD had made a covenant with them and commanded them, “Do not fear other gods, or bow down to them, or serve them, or sacrifice to them, but fear the LORD, who brought you up from the land of Egypt with great power and an outstretched arm. Bow down to him, and sacrifice to him. Be careful always to keep the statutes and the rulings, the law and the commandment that he wrote for you, and do not fear other gods. Do not forget the covenant I made with you, and do not fear other gods. Fear the LORD your God instead, and he will rescue you from the power of all your enemies.” But they would not listen; they kept to their former custom. So these nations feared the LORD and also served their idols. Their children and their grandchildren have done as their ancestors did, to this day.

fields.title: 2 Kings 18
fields.body_html:
Hezekiah king of Judah

In the third year of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz king of Judah became king. He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Abi daughter of Zechariah. He did what was right in the sight of the LORD, in every way as his ancestor David had done. He removed the high places, broke the standing stones and cut down the Asherah pole. He also smashed to pieces the bronze snake that Moses had made, for until that time the Israelites had been burning incense to it. It was called Nehushtan. He trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel. Among all the kings of Judah there was no one like him, either after him or among those who were before him. He held fast to the LORD and did not turn away from following him. He kept the commandments the LORD had given to Moses. The LORD was with him, and he succeeded in everything he set out to do. He rebelled against the king of Assyria and would not serve him. He defeated the Philistines as far as Gaza and its territory, from watchtower to fortified city.

The fall of Samaria

In the fourth year of King Hezekiah, which was the seventh year of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel, Shalmaneser king of Assyria marched against Samaria and laid siege to it. At the end of three years they captured it. Samaria was taken in the sixth year of Hezekiah, which was the ninth year of Hoshea king of Israel. The king of Assyria carried the Israelites away into exile to Assyria. He led them away to live in Halah, on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes. This happened because they did not obey the voice of the LORD their God, but broke his covenant, everything Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded. They would neither listen nor do it.

Sennacherib invades Judah

In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria marched against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them. Then Hezekiah king of Judah sent a message to Lachish, to the king of Assyria: “I have done wrong. Withdraw from me, and I will bear whatever you lay on me.” The king of Assyria required Hezekiah king of Judah to pay about 11 tons of silver and about 2,250 pounds of gold. Hezekiah handed over to him all the silver to be found in the LORD’s house and in the treasuries of the king’s palace. At that time Hezekiah stripped the gold from the doors of the LORD’s temple and from the doorposts that he, Hezekiah king of Judah, had covered with it, and gave it to the king of Assyria.

The Assyrian officers at Jerusalem

Then the king of Assyria sent the commander-in-chief, the chief of the court officials and the chief officer from Lachish to King Hezekiah in Jerusalem, with a large army. They went up and came to Jerusalem. When they arrived, they took their stand by the water channel from the Upper Pool, which is on the road to the Fuller’s Field. They called for the king, and Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was in charge of the palace, went out to them, together with Shebna the secretary and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder. Then the chief officer said to them, “Tell Hezekiah, ‘The great king, the king of Assyria, says this: What sort of confidence is this that you are trusting in? You claim to have a strategy and strength for war, but those are nothing but empty words. Who is it you are leaning on, that you have rebelled against me? Now look, you are leaning on Egypt, this cracked reed you use for a staff. Anyone who puts weight on it will have it run into the hand and pierce it. That is what Pharaoh king of Egypt is to all who rely on him. Or if you tell me, “Our trust is in the LORD our God,” did Hezekiah not get rid of his high places and his altars? Did he not tell Judah and Jerusalem, “It is before this altar in Jerusalem that you must bow down”? Come, then, place a bet with my master the king of Assyria. I will hand you 2,000 horses, if you can supply men to ride them! Then how could you drive off a single governor, one of my master’s lowest officials? Yet you put your trust in Egypt to send chariots and horsemen! Now, was it apart from the LORD that I came up against this place to ruin it? It was the LORD who said to me, “Go up against this land and ruin it.”‘” Eliakim son of Hilkiah, Shebna, and Joah said to the chief officer, “We beg you, use Aramaic when you talk with your servants, because we know it. Do not talk with us in the language of Judah while the people on the wall are listening.” But the chief officer replied to them, “Did my master send me to speak these words just to you and your master? No, they are for the men who sit on the wall, who are going to eat their own dung and drink their own urine along with you!” Then the chief officer stood and shouted in the language of Judah: “Listen to the word of the great king, the king of Assyria! The king says this: ‘Do not let Hezekiah fool you. He has no power to rescue you from the king’s hand. And do not let Hezekiah lead you to rely on the LORD when he tells you, “The LORD is sure to rescue us. The king of Assyria will never be given this city.”‘ Do not listen to Hezekiah. The king of Assyria says this: ‘Come to terms with me and surrender to me. Then everyone may eat from their own vine and their own fig tree and drink water from their own cistern, until I come to move you to a country like your own, a country of grain and fresh wine, of bread and vineyards, of olive oil and honey. Then you will live and not die. Do not listen to Hezekiah, for he is leading you astray when he says, “The LORD will rescue us.” Did any of the gods of the nations ever rescue its own land from the hand of the king of Assyria? Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Did they rescue Samaria from my hand? Among all the gods of the lands, which ones have rescued their land from my hand, that the LORD should rescue Jerusalem from me?’” The people stayed silent and did not say a word in reply, for the king had given an order: “Do not answer him.” Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was in charge of the palace, Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder, went to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and reported to him what the chief officer had said.

fields.title: 2 Kings 19
fields.body_html:
Hezekiah sends to Isaiah

As soon as King Hezekiah heard it, he tore his clothes, wrapped himself in sackcloth, and entered the house of the LORD. He sent Eliakim, who was in charge of the palace, Shebna the secretary, and the senior priests, all clothed in sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz. They said to him, “Hezekiah says this: Today is a day of distress, of rebuke and of disgrace. Children have reached the opening of the womb, and there is no strength to bring them to birth. Perhaps the LORD your God will hear everything the chief officer said when his master the king of Assyria sent him to insult the living God, and will call him to account for the words the LORD your God has heard. Lift up a prayer, then, for the remnant that is still here.” So King Hezekiah’s officials came to Isaiah. Isaiah said to them, “Say to your master, ‘The LORD says this: Do not be frightened by what you have heard, the words with which the king of Assyria’s lackeys have reviled me. I am about to put a spirit in him: he will hear a rumor and go back to his own country, and in his own country I will make him fall by the sword.’” The chief officer went back and found the king of Assyria attacking Libnah, for he had heard that the king had left Lachish. Then the king heard that Tirhakah king of Cush was marching out to fight against him. So he sent messengers to Hezekiah again, saying, “Say this to Hezekiah king of Judah: ‘Do not let your God, the one you rely on, deceive you by saying, “Jerusalem will not be handed over to the king of Assyria.” You yourself have heard how the kings of Assyria dealt with all the lands, wiping them out. And you expect to escape? Did the gods of the nations my forefathers destroyed rescue them, Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden in Telassar? Where is the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of the city of Sepharvaim, of Hena, or of Ivvah?’” Hezekiah took the letter from the messengers’ hand and read it through. He went up to the house of the LORD and opened it out in the presence of the LORD.

Hezekiah’s prayer

Then Hezekiah prayed before the LORD: “LORD, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim: you, and no one else, are God of every kingdom on earth. It was you who made the heavens and the earth. Turn your ear, LORD, and listen; open your eyes, LORD, and look. Hear the words of Sennacherib, who has sent his envoy to insult the living God. It is true, LORD, that the kings of Assyria have devastated the nations and their lands, and have flung their gods into the fire. Those were never gods, only wood and stone shaped by human hands, so they could destroy them. So now, LORD our God, please rescue us from his power, so that every kingdom on earth will know that you, LORD, alone are God.”

Isaiah’s answer

Then Isaiah son of Amoz sent word to Hezekiah: “The LORD, the God of Israel, says this: I have heard your prayer to me about Sennacherib king of Assyria.
This is the word the LORD has spoken against him:
The virgin, Daughter Zion, looks down on you and laughs at you;
Daughter Jerusalem shakes her head at your back.
Do you know whom you have mocked and reviled?
At whom did you shout,
at whom did you lift your haughty eyes? At the Holy One of Israel!
Through your messengers you have mocked the Lord.
You said, ‘With chariots past counting I have climbed the mountain heights, the far ridges of Lebanon.
I will fell its loftiest cedars and its finest junipers.
I will enter its most distant camping place and its lush forest.
I have dug wells and drunk foreign water,
and under the tread of my feet every stream of Egypt will run dry.’
Have you not heard? I did this long ago;
in days of old I shaped it.
Now I have made it happen,
so that you turn walled cities into heaps of rubble.
Their people were powerless,
terrified and put to shame.
They were like the plants of the open field and fresh green herbs,
like grass on a rooftop, scorched before it can stand tall.
I know where you sit, when you go out and when you come in,
and how you storm against me.
Since you rage against me
and your arrogance has come up to my ears,
I will set my hook in your nose and my bit between your lips,
and I will lead you back along the same road by which you came.
Here is the sign for you:
this year you will live on grain that sprang up untended,
and next year on whatever comes up after it;
but in the third year, sow and harvest, plant vineyards and eat what they bear.
Those of the house of Judah who escape and are left will once more put down roots below
and bear fruit above.
For a remnant will go out from Jerusalem,
and from Mount Zion those who have escaped.
The burning zeal of the LORD of Armies will make this happen.

The Assyrian army is struck down

Therefore the LORD says this about the king of Assyria:
He will never set foot in this city.
He will not fire a single arrow into it,
nor face it with a shield,
nor pile up an earthen ramp against its walls.
The road that brought him here will take him back again.
This city he will not enter, declares the LORD.
I will shield this city and rescue it,
for my own sake and for my servant David’s sake.”
That night the angel of the LORD went out into the Assyrian camp and struck down 185,000. At dawn, when people got up, they found them all lying dead. So Sennacherib king of Assyria struck camp and went away. He returned home and stayed in Nineveh. While he was bowing down in the house of Nisroch his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer, his own sons, cut him down with the sword and fled to the land of Ararat. Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place.

fields.title: 2 Kings 20
fields.body_html:
Hezekiah’s illness

In those days Hezekiah fell ill and was close to death. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz came to him and said, “The LORD says this: Give final instructions to your household, for you are dying and will not live.” Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall and prayed to the LORD: “Please, LORD, remember how I have lived before you faithfully and with an undivided heart, doing what is good in your sight.” And Hezekiah wept loudly.

Isaiah had not yet left the middle courtyard when the word of the LORD came to him: “Go back and say to Hezekiah, the ruler of my people, ‘The LORD, the God of your ancestor David, says this: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. I am about to heal you, and on the third day you will go up to the house of the LORD. I will add fifteen years to your days. I will rescue you and this city from the grasp of the king of Assyria, and I will shield this city for my own sake and for my servant David’s sake.’” Then Isaiah said, “Bring a lump of pressed figs.” They brought it and spread it on the sore, and he recovered. Hezekiah had asked Isaiah, “What sign will there be that the LORD is going to heal me, and that on the third day I will go up to the house of the LORD?” Isaiah answered, “This will be your sign from the LORD that the LORD will carry out what he has said: Should the shadow go forward ten steps, or should it go back ten steps?” Hezekiah answered, “It is easy for the shadow to lengthen ten steps. No, let the shadow go back ten steps.” Then the prophet Isaiah called out to the LORD, and he made the shadow go back ten steps, back up the steps of Ahaz that it had gone down.

Envoys from Babylon

About that time Berodach-baladan son of Baladan, the king of Babylon, sent letters and a present to Hezekiah, because he had heard that Hezekiah had been ill. Hezekiah listened to them and showed them his whole treasury: the silver and the gold, the spices and the fine oil, his armory, and everything to be found in his storehouses. In his palace and across his whole kingdom, there was nothing he did not let them see. Then the prophet Isaiah came to King Hezekiah and asked him, “What did these men say? And where did they come from to visit you?” Hezekiah answered, “They came from a faraway country, from Babylon.” He asked, “What did they see in your palace?” Hezekiah replied, “They saw all that is in my palace. In my storerooms there is not a thing I failed to show them.” Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Listen to the word of the LORD: Look, a time is coming when all that is in your palace, everything your ancestors have laid up until today, will be hauled off to Babylon. Not one thing will remain, says the LORD. Some of your descendants, born of your own line, will be taken away, and they will serve as eunuchs in the palace of the Babylonian king.” Hezekiah answered Isaiah, “This word of the LORD that you have brought is good.” He was thinking, “Is it not good, if there will be peace and stability as long as I live?” The rest of the acts of Hezekiah, all his might, and the pool and the conduit he made to bring water into the city, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Judah. Then Hezekiah rested with his ancestors, and his son Manasseh became king in his place.

fields.title: 2 Kings 21
fields.body_html:
Manasseh king of Judah

Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Hephzibah. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, following the detestable practices of the nations that the LORD had driven out ahead of the Israelites. He rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had destroyed. He set up altars for Baal and made an Asherah pole, as Ahab king of Israel had done. He bowed down to all the host of heaven and served them. He built altars in the house of the LORD, the house about which the LORD had said, “In Jerusalem I will put my name.” He built altars to all the host of heaven in the two courtyards of the house of the LORD. He made his son pass through the fire, practiced fortune-telling and read omens, and consulted a medium and spiritists. He did much evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger. He placed the carved Asherah image he had made in the house about which the LORD had said to David and to his son Solomon, “In this house, and in Jerusalem, the city I chose from among all the tribes of Israel, I will put my name forever. And I will not again make the feet of Israel wander from the land I gave to their ancestors, if only they will be careful to do all that I have commanded them, all the law that my servant Moses commanded them.” But they did not listen. Manasseh led them astray, so that they did more evil than the nations the LORD had destroyed ahead of the Israelites. The LORD spoke through his servants the prophets, saying, “Because Manasseh king of Judah has done these detestable things, doing more evil than all that the Amorites did before him, and has also made Judah sin with his idols,

therefore the LORD, the God of Israel, says this: Look, I am about to bring such disaster on Jerusalem and Judah that it will make both ears of all who hear of it tingle. I will stretch over Jerusalem the measuring line used on Samaria and the plumb line used on the house of Ahab. I will wipe Jerusalem clean as someone wipes a dish, wiping it and turning it upside down. I will abandon what is left of my own people and hand them over to their enemies, and they will become plunder and spoil for all their enemies, because they have done what is evil in my sight and have kept on provoking me to anger from the day their ancestors came out of Egypt until this day.” Manasseh also shed so much innocent blood that he filled Jerusalem with it from one end to the other. This was besides the sin he led Judah into, so that they did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. The rest of the acts of Manasseh, all that he did and the sin he committed, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Judah. Then Manasseh rested with his ancestors and was buried in the garden of his palace, the garden of Uzza. His son Amon became king in his place.

Amon king of Judah

Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned two years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Meshullemeth daughter of Haruz, from Jotbah. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as his father Manasseh had done. He followed every path his father had followed. He served the idols his father had served and bowed down to them. He abandoned the LORD, the God of his ancestors, and did not walk in the way of the LORD. Amon’s officials plotted against him and killed the king in his palace. Then the people of the land killed all who had plotted against King Amon, and the people of the land made his son Josiah king in his place. The rest of the acts of Amon, what he did, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Judah. Amon was laid in his tomb in the garden of Uzza, and his son Josiah became king in his place.

fields.title: 2 Kings 22
fields.body_html:
Josiah king of Judah

Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jedidah daughter of Adaiah from Bozkath. He did what was right in the sight of the LORD and walked in all the way of his ancestor David. He did not turn aside to the right or to the left.

The book of the law is found

In the eighteenth year of King Josiah, the king sent the secretary Shaphan son of Azaliah, son of Meshullam, to the house of the LORD, saying, “Go up to Hilkiah the high priest and have him count up the money brought into the house of the LORD, the money the doorkeepers have taken in from the people, and have them hand it to the men doing the work, who have been put in charge of the house of the LORD. Let these pay it to the workmen in the house of the LORD who are repairing the damage to the house, to the craftsmen, the builders and the masons, and let them buy timber and dressed stone to repair the house. But no accounting is to be asked of them for the money handed to them, because they deal honestly.” Hilkiah the high priest said to Shaphan the secretary, “In the house of the LORD I have found the book of the law.” Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it. Shaphan the secretary went to the king and reported to him, “Your officials have emptied out the money found in the house and handed it over to the men doing the work, who have been put in charge of the house of the LORD.” Then Shaphan the secretary told the king, “Hilkiah the priest has handed me a book.” And Shaphan read it aloud to the king. When the king heard the words written in the book of the law, he tore his clothes. Then the king gave orders to Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Achbor son of Micaiah, Shaphan the secretary and Asaiah the king’s official, “Go and ask the LORD on my behalf, and on behalf of the people and all Judah, about the words of this book that has been found. The LORD’s anger burns hot against us, because our ancestors did not listen to the words of this book or do all that it lays down for us.” So Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan and Asaiah went to the prophet Huldah, the wife of Shallum son of Tikvah, son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe. Her home was in the Second Quarter of Jerusalem, and they spoke with her. She said to them, “The LORD, the God of Israel, says this: Tell the man who sent you to me, ‘The LORD says this: I am about to bring disaster on this place and on those who live in it, all the words in the book the king of Judah has read, because they have abandoned me and burned incense to other gods, provoking me to anger with all the work of their hands. So my wrath will blaze against this place, and it will not be put out.’ But to the king of Judah, who sent you to ask the LORD, say this: ‘The LORD, the God of Israel, says this: As for the words you have heard, because your heart was tender, and when you heard what I spoke against this place and its people, that they would become a horror and a curse, you humbled yourself before the LORD; and because you tore your clothes and wept before me, I in turn have heard you, declares the LORD. Therefore I will gather you to your ancestors, and you will be gathered to your grave in peace. You will not see with your own eyes all the disaster I am going to bring on this place.’” Then they took her answer back to the king.

fields.title: 2 Kings 23
fields.body_html:
Josiah renews the covenant

Then the king sent word, and all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem were gathered to him. The king went up to the house of the LORD, and with him went all the people of Judah and all who lived in Jerusalem, the priests and the prophets, and all the people, from the least to the greatest. In their hearing he read out all the words of the book of the covenant, which had been found in the house of the LORD. The king stood by the pillar and made the covenant in the presence of the LORD: to follow the LORD and to keep his commandments, his decrees and his statutes with all his heart and all his being, and so to carry out the words of this covenant written in this book. And all the people committed themselves to the covenant. The king ordered Hilkiah the high priest, the priests next in rank and the keepers of the threshold to bring out of the temple of the LORD all the objects made for Baal, for Asherah and for all the host of heaven. He burned them outside Jerusalem in the fields of the Kidron Valley and carried their ashes to Bethel. He did away with the idolatrous priests whom the kings of Judah had appointed to burn incense at the high places in the towns of Judah and around Jerusalem, and with those who burned incense to Baal, to the sun and the moon, to the constellations and to all the host of heaven. He took the Asherah pole out of the house of the LORD to the Kidron Valley outside Jerusalem. He burned it there in the Kidron Valley, ground it to dust and threw the dust on the graves of the common people. He tore down the quarters of the male shrine prostitutes in the house of the LORD, where the women wove coverings for Asherah. He brought all the priests in from the towns of Judah and defiled the high places where those priests had burned incense, from Geba to Beersheba. He broke down the high places of the gates that stood at the way into the Gate of Joshua, the city governor, on the left as one enters the city gate. The priests of the high places did not serve at the altar of the LORD in Jerusalem, but they ate unleavened bread with their fellow priests. He defiled Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom, so that no one would ever again make a son or daughter pass through the fire for Molech. He removed the horses the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun from the entrance to the house of the LORD, by the room of Nathan-melech the official, which was in the precincts. And he burned up the chariots of the sun. The king pulled down the altars that the kings of Judah had made on the roof of the upper room of Ahaz, and the altars Manasseh had built in the two courts of the house of the LORD. He broke them in pieces and removed them from there, and he threw their dust into the Kidron Valley. The king defiled the high places east of Jerusalem, south of the Mount of Destruction, which Solomon king of Israel had built for Ashtoreth the detestable goddess of the Sidonians, for Chemosh the detestable god of Moab, and for Milcom the detestable god of the Ammonites. He smashed the standing stones, cut down the Asherah poles, and filled the places where they had stood with human bones. Even the altar at Bethel, the high place made by Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel to sin, even that altar and high place he tore down. He burned the high place and crushed it to dust, and he burned the Asherah pole. As Josiah turned around, he saw the tombs there on the hillside, and he sent men to take the bones out of the tombs. He burned them on the altar and so defiled it, in keeping with the word of the LORD that the man of God had cried out when he foretold these things. He asked, “What is that grave marker I see?” The men of the town answered, “The man of God who came from Judah is buried there. He cried out against the altar of Bethel the very things you have done.” “Leave him in peace,” he said. “Let no one disturb his bones.” So they spared his bones, together with the bones of the prophet who had come from Samaria. Josiah also removed every shrine on the high places in the towns of Samaria, which the kings of Israel had made, provoking the LORD to anger. He did to them just what he had done at Bethel. He sacrificed all the priests of the high places who were there on the altars, and he burned human bones on them. Then he went back to Jerusalem. The king commanded all the people, “Keep the Passover to the LORD your God in the way that is written in this book of the covenant.” No Passover like this had been kept since the time of the judges who judged Israel, nor through all the time of the kings of Israel and the kings of Judah. But this Passover was kept to the LORD in Jerusalem in the eighteenth year of King Josiah. Josiah also purged the mediums and the spiritists, the household gods, the idols and all the detestable things to be seen in the land of Judah and in Jerusalem. He did this so as to carry out the words of the law, as they were written in the book Hilkiah the priest had discovered in the house of the LORD. Before him there was no king like him, who turned to the LORD with his whole heart, with his whole being, and with all his strength, in keeping with all the law of Moses; and after him no one like him arose. Even so, the LORD did not turn away from the fierceness of his great anger, which burned against Judah because of all the ways Manasseh had provoked him. The LORD said, “I will remove Judah from my sight too, as I removed Israel. I will reject this city I chose, Jerusalem, and the house of which I said, ‘My name will be there.’” The rest of the acts of Josiah, and all that he did, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Judah. In his days Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt went up to the king of Assyria at the Euphrates River, and King Josiah marched out to meet him. When Neco saw him, he killed him at Megiddo. His officials carried his body in a chariot from Megiddo and brought him to Jerusalem, where they buried him in his own tomb. The people of the land then took Jehoahaz son of Josiah; they anointed him and made him king in place of his father.

Jehoahaz king of Judah

Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, just as his ancestors had done. Pharaoh Neco put him in chains at Riblah in the land of Hamath, so that he could no longer reign in Jerusalem, and he imposed on the land a payment of about 7,500 pounds of silver and about 75 pounds of gold. Pharaoh Neco made Eliakim son of Josiah king in the place of Josiah his father. He changed Eliakim’s name to Jehoiakim. Jehoahaz, though, he took away, and Jehoahaz went to Egypt and died there. Jehoiakim paid Pharaoh the silver and the gold, but to raise the money Pharaoh demanded he had to tax the land. He exacted the silver and gold from the people of the land, each paying the amount assessed, to give to Pharaoh Neco.

Jehoiakim king of Judah

Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Zebudah daughter of Pedaiah from Rumah. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, just as his ancestors had done.

fields.title: 2 Kings 24
fields.body_html:
Jehoiakim and Babylon

In Jehoiakim’s days Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up, and Jehoiakim became his vassal for three years. Then he turned and rebelled against him. The LORD sent raiding bands of Chaldeans, Arameans, Moabites and Ammonites against him. He sent them against Judah to destroy it, in keeping with the word the LORD had spoken through his servants the prophets. Surely it was at the command of the LORD that this came upon Judah, to put them away from his presence because of Manasseh’s sins, all that he had done, and also because of the innocent blood he had shed. He had filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the LORD was not willing to forgive. The rest of the acts of Jehoiakim, and all that he did, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Judah. Jehoiakim rested with his ancestors, and his son Jehoiachin became king in his place. The king of Egypt did not again march out from his own land, for the king of Babylon had taken everything that had belonged to the king of Egypt, from the Wadi of Egypt to the Euphrates River.

Jehoiachin is taken to Babylon

Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Nehushta daughter of Elnathan from Jerusalem. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, just as his father had done. At that time the officers of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon advanced on Jerusalem, and the city came under siege. Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to the city himself while his officers were besieging it. Jehoiachin king of Judah went out to the king of Babylon in surrender, he and his mother, his servants, his officials and his court officers. The king of Babylon took him prisoner in the eighth year of his reign. He carried off from there all the treasures of the house of the LORD and those of the king’s palace, and he cut up all the gold vessels that Solomon king of Israel had made for the temple of the LORD, just as the LORD had said. He carried all Jerusalem into exile: all the officials and all the mighty warriors, 10,000 captives, and all the craftsmen and smiths. No one was left except the poorest people of the land. He carried Jehoiachin into exile to Babylon. The king’s mother, the king’s wives, his court officers and the leading men of the land he also took into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon. The king of Babylon brought to Babylon as exiles all the men of valor, 7,000, and the craftsmen and smiths, a thousand, all of them strong men fit for war. The king of Babylon made Jehoiachin’s uncle Mattaniah king in his place and changed his name to Zedekiah.

Zedekiah king of Judah

Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, just as Jehoiakim had done. It was because of the anger of the LORD that all this happened in Jerusalem and Judah, until he cast them out of his presence. And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

fields.title: 2 Kings 25
fields.body_html:
The fall of Jerusalem

On the tenth day of the tenth month, in the ninth year of Zedekiah’s reign, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon advanced on Jerusalem with his whole army. He camped against the city, and they built siege works against it on every side. The city was under siege until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah. By the ninth day of the fourth month the city was gripped by famine, and the people of the land had no food. Then the city wall was breached, and all the soldiers fled by night through the gate between the two walls near the king’s garden, though the Chaldeans were all around the city. The king went off toward the Arabah. But the Chaldean army chased the king and caught up with him in the plains of Jericho, and his whole army scattered away from him. They seized the king and took him up to Riblah, to the king of Babylon, and there they passed sentence on him. They slaughtered Zedekiah’s sons while he watched. Then the king of Babylon put out Zedekiah’s eyes, bound him in bronze fetters and took him to Babylon.

The temple is burned

In the fifth month, on the seventh day, the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar’s reign over Babylon, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, an official of the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem. He burned the house of the LORD, the king’s palace and all the houses of Jerusalem; every important house he burned down. The whole Chaldean army that was with the captain of the guard tore down the walls all around Jerusalem. Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried into exile the rest of the people who were left in the city, those who had deserted to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the population. But the captain of the guard left some of the poorest people of the land to tend the vineyards and work the fields. The Chaldeans broke up the bronze pillars that were in the house of the LORD, the stands, and the bronze Sea that was in the house of the LORD, and they hauled the metal off to Babylon. They also took away the pots, the shovels, the wick trimmers, the dishes and all the bronze utensils used in the temple service. The captain of the guard took away the firepans and the sprinkling bowls, everything that was made of gold and everything that was made of silver. As for the two pillars, the one Sea and the stands Solomon made for the house of the LORD, the bronze of all these things was more than could be weighed. One pillar was about 27 feet high, with a bronze capital on top of it. The capital was about 4 1/2 feet high, with a network and pomegranates all around it, all of bronze. The second pillar, with its network, was the same. The captain of the guard also seized Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the priest next to him, and the three doorkeepers. From the city he took an official who had been in charge of the soldiers, five of the king’s advisers who were found in the city, the secretary of the commander of the army, who mustered the people of the land for war, and sixty of the people of the land who were still in the city. Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard led them away to Riblah and brought them before the king of Babylon. The king of Babylon had them struck down and executed at Riblah, in the land of Hamath. So Judah went into exile, away from its own land. Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, governor over the people he had left in the land of Judah.

Gedaliah at Mizpah

All the commanders of the forces and their men learned that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah, and they came to Gedaliah at Mizpah. They were Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah son of the Maacathite, together with their men. Gedaliah swore an oath to them and their men. “Do not be afraid of the Chaldean officials,” he said. “Settle in the land, serve the king of Babylon, and all will go well with you.”

But in the seventh month Ishmael son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama, who was of royal descent, came with ten men and struck down Gedaliah and killed him, together with the Judeans and the Chaldeans who were with him at Mizpah. Then all the people, from the least to the greatest, and the commanders of the forces set out and went to Egypt, because they were afraid of the Chaldeans.

Jehoiachin is released

In the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month, Evil-Merodach king of Babylon, in the year he became king, showed favor to Jehoiachin king of Judah and released him from prison. He spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat of honor above the seats of the other kings who were with him in Babylon. So Jehoiachin put off his prison clothes, and for the rest of his life he ate regularly at the king’s table. And the king gave him a regular allowance, a portion for each day, all the days of his life.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
And the king gave him a regular allowance, a portion for each day, all the days of his life.

— 2 Kings 25:30

2 Kings ends with a meal. The temple is ash, the walls of Jerusalem are rubble, the people are scattered from Egypt to Babylon, and the last word is about a captive king eating his daily bread at a foreign table. It is a very small hope, but the book chose to end on it.

The question the book leaves with you

The first readers of 2 Kings had lost everything the earlier books had promised: the land, the city, the temple, the throne. They would have asked whether God had failed. Kings answers no. It says, over and over, that the end came because the people would not listen, and that it came only after centuries of warnings: “Yet the LORD warned Israel and Judah through every prophet and every seer.” Judgement was not God breaking his word but keeping it.

But that is not the only thing Kings says. The same God who sent the prophets also kept a lamp burning for David when every king of Judah seemed bent on putting it out. He hid one child in the temple for six years. He was “gracious to them and had compassion on them” when they deserved neither. And he kept Jehoiachin alive in Babylon. So the question the book leaves is not only “Why did this happen?” but “What will God do now with the promise he made to David?”

The book does not say. It simply shows a son of David out of his prison clothes, eating at a king’s table. Readers who know the rest of the Bible see more in that scene than its first readers could.

Where the story goes next

The story of the exile is told from the inside by the prophets who lived it, Jeremiah in Jerusalem and Ezekiel among the captives in Babylon, and its end is told in 2 Chronicles and Ezra. Jeremiah had said the exile would last seventy years: “When Babylon’s seventy years have been completed, I will come to your aid.” Chronicles ends with Cyrus of Persia telling the exiles to go home and rebuild, and Ezra tells how they did.

And the line of Jehoiachin did not end in Babylon. Matthew’s Gospel opens with the family tree of Jesus, and when it reaches the end of Kings it names this very king, under another form of his name:

After the deportation to Babylon, Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel of Zerubbabel. Zerubbabel was the father of Abiud, Abiud of Eliakim, and Eliakim of Azor. Azor was the father of Zadok, Zadok of Achim, and Achim of Eliud. Eliud was the father of Eleazar, Eleazar of Matthan, and Matthan of Jacob. Jacob was the father of Joseph, the husband of Mary, and of Mary was born Jesus, who is called Christ.

— Matthew 1:12–16

Matthew counts the generations in three sets of fourteen, “fourteen from David to the deportation to Babylon, and fourteen from the deportation to Babylon to Christ.” The exile is not the end of David’s story but its turning point.

Elijah and Elisha, too, walk into the Gospels. Jesus began his ministry at Nazareth by recalling the widow of Zarephath and Naaman the Syrian, foreigners to whom the prophets were sent (Luke 4:25–27). He fed crowds with a few loaves, raised a widow’s son and touched lepers, and his disciples saw the God of Elijah at work in him.

Where to go from here

2 Kings has given preachers some of their favourite texts. A few places to begin:

  • On Elijah’s cloak and Elisha’s double portion (2 Kings 2). D. L. Moody’s Secret Power, whose chapter “Power: In and Upon” follows Elisha across the Jordan.
  • On the widow’s oil (2 Kings 4:1–7). Alexander Maclaren’s sermon When the Oil Flows (2 Kings 4:6), on God giving as long as we bring something he can fill; and “The Borrower’s Chains”, a chapter of Faithful with Little, an Ochorus Original, which reads the same story as a lesson about debt.
  • On the Shunammite’s son (2 Kings 4:8–37). Charles H. Spurgeon’s The Soul-Winner, whose chapter “How to Raise the Dead” draws from Elisha’s prayer over the child lessons for everyone who longs to bring others to life in Christ.
  • On Naaman (2 Kings 5). D. L. Moody’s sermon Naaman the Syrian, on pride, plain obedience and the cleansing no rank can buy.
  • On Jehu and Jehonadab (2 Kings 10:15). John Wesley’s sermon Catholic Spirit, which builds a doctrine of Christian love across differences of opinion on Jehu’s question, “Is your heart right with mine, as my heart is with yours?”
  • On Hezekiah (2 Kings 18–20). E. M. Bounds’s Prayer and Praying Men, with its chapter “Hezekiah, the Praying King”; and “Opening the Letter Before the Lord”, a chapter of The Prayers Jesus Learned, an Ochorus Original, on 2 Kings 19:14–19.
  • On the whole story of the divided kingdom. Hannah Whitall Smith’s Old Testament Types and Teachings, whose chapter “2 Kings and 2 Chronicles: The Divided Kingdom” reads it as a warning against carelessness after seasons of blessing.
  • For younger readers. Tell Me the Story – Book 3: Kings and Prophets, an Ochorus Original, with its stories of the chariots of fire, Naaman washing seven times, and Josiah, the boy king.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to 2 Kings in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

And remember, when the story seems darkest, what Elisha said to a frightened servant who saw only the army at the gates:

“Do not be afraid,” Elisha answered. “There are more with us than there are with them.”

— 2 Kings 6:16
